From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Unrestricted availability of scholarly publications

Not to be confused with [Open source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_source "Open source").

For other uses, see [Open access (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access_(disambiguation) "Open access (disambiguation)").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Open_Access_logo_PLoS_transparent.svg/250px-Open_Access_logo_PLoS_transparent.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Open_Access_logo_PLoS_transparent.svg)

Open access logo, originally designed by [Public Library of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Library_of_Science "Public Library of Science")

[Video 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/71/PhD_Comics_Open_Access_Week_2012.ogv?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

A [_PhD Comics_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piled_Higher_and_Deeper "Piled Higher and Deeper") introduction to open access

**Open access** (**OA**) is a set of principles and a range of practices through which nominally [copyrightable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright "Copyright") publications are delivered to readers free of access charges or other barriers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-suber_overview-1) With open access strictly defined (according to the 2001 definition), or [libre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gratis_versus_libre "Gratis versus libre") open access, barriers to copying or reuse are also reduced or removed by applying an [open license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_license "Open license") for copyright, which regulates post-publication uses of the work.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-suber_overview-1)

The main focus of the open access movement has been on [peer reviewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer_review "Peer review") research literature, and more specifically on [academic journals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal "Academic journal").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:0-2) This is because:

*   such publications [have been](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal_publishing_reform "Academic journal publishing reform") a subject of [serials crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serials_crisis "Serials crisis"), unlike [newspapers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newspaper "Newspaper"), [magazines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine "Magazine") and [fiction writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiction_writing "Fiction writing"). The main difference between these two groups is in [demand elasticity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demand_elasticity "Demand elasticity"): whereas an English literature curriculum can substitute _[Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry\_Potter\_and\_the\_Philosopher's\_Stone "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone")_ with a public domain alternative, such as _[A Voyage to Lilliput](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulliver's\_Travels "Gulliver's Travels"),_ an [emergency room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_room "Emergency room")[physician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physician "Physician") treating a patient for a life-threatening [urushiol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urushiol "Urushiol") poisoning cannot substitute the most recent, but [paywalled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paywalled "Paywalled") review article on this topic[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-3) with a 90-year-old copyright-expired article[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-4) that was published before the invention of [prednisone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prednisone "Prednisone") in 1954.

*   the authors of research papers are not paid in any way, so they do not suffer any monetary losses, when they switch from [behind paywall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serials_crisis#Big_deal "Serials crisis") to open access publishing, especially, if they use [diamond open access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond_open_access "Diamond open access") media.

*   the cost of [electronic publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_publishing "Electronic publishing"), which has been the main form of distribution of [journal articles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journals "Academic journals") since c.2000, is incommensurably smaller than the cost of on-paper publishing and distribution, which is still preferred by many readers of fiction.

Whereas non-open access journals cover publishing costs through [access tolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subscription_business_model "Subscription business model") such as subscriptions, site licenses or [pay-per-view](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pay-per-view "Pay-per-view") charges, open-access journals are characterised by funding models which do not require the reader to pay to read the journal's contents, relying instead on [author fees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Author_fees "Author fees") or on public funding, subsidies and sponsorships. Open access can be applied to all forms of published research output, including [peer-reviewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer-reviewed "Peer-reviewed") and non peer-reviewed [academic journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal "Academic journal") articles, [conference papers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conference_papers "Conference papers"), [theses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theses "Theses"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-5) book chapters,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-suber_overview-1)[monographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monograph "Monograph"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-6)[research reports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_report "Research report") and images.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-esatc-7)

## Definitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Definitions")]

There are different models of open access publishing and publishers may use one or more of these models.

### Colour naming system

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Colour naming system")]

Different open access types are currently commonly described using a colour system. The most commonly recognised names are "green", "gold", and "hybrid" open access; however, several other models and alternative terms are also used.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-8)

#### Gold OA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Gold OA")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/DOAJ_growth.png/250px-DOAJ_growth.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DOAJ_growth.png)

Number of gold open access journals listed in the [Directory of Open Access Journals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directory_of_Open_Access_Journals "Directory of Open Access Journals")[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-10)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/PMC_growth.png/250px-PMC_growth.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PMC_growth.png)

Number of gold and hybrid open access journals listed in [PubMed Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PubMed_Central "PubMed Central")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-12)

In the gold OA model, the publisher makes all articles and related content available for free immediately on the journal's website. In such publications, articles are licensed for sharing and reuse via [Creative Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Commons "Creative Commons") licenses or similar.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-suber_overview-1)

Many gold OA publishers charge an [article processing charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_processing_charge "Article processing charge") (APC), which is typically paid through institutional or grant funding. The majority of gold open access journals charging APCs follow an "author-pays" model,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-13) although this is not an intrinsic property of gold OA.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Eve_pp._1%E2%80%9342-14)

#### Green OA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Green OA")]

[Self-archiving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-archiving "Self-archiving") by authors is permitted under green OA. Independently from publication by a publisher, the author also posts the work to a website controlled by the author, the research institution that funded or hosted the work, or to an independent central open repository, where people can download the work without paying.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Gadd-15)

Green OA is free of charge for the author. Some publishers (less than 5% and decreasing as of 2014) may charge a fee for an additional service[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Gadd-15) such as a [free license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_license "Free license") on the publisher-authored copyrightable portions of the printed version of an article.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-16)

If the author posts the near-final version of their work after peer review by a journal, the archived version is called a "[postprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postprint "Postprint")". This can be the accepted manuscript as returned by the journal to the author after successful peer review.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-17)

#### Hybrid OA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Hybrid OA")]

[Hybrid open-access journals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hybrid_open-access_journal "Hybrid open-access journal") contain a mixture of open access articles and closed access articles.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-19) A publisher following this model is partially funded by subscriptions, and only provide open access for those individual articles for which the authors (or research sponsor) pay a publication fee.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Suber2012-20) Hybrid OA generally costs more than gold OA and can offer a lower quality of service.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-auto-21) A particularly controversial practice in hybrid open access journals is "[double dipping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_dipping_(publishing) "Double dipping (publishing)")", where both authors and subscribers are charged.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Open_access_double_dipping_policy-22) For these reasons, hybrid open access journals have been called a "[Mephistophelian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mephistophelian "Mephistophelian") invention",[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-23) and publishing in hybrid OA journals often do not qualify for funding under [open access mandates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access_mandate "Open access mandate"), as libraries already pay for subscriptions thus have no financial incentive to fund open access articles in such journals.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-24)

#### Bronze OA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Bronze OA")]

Bronze open access articles are free to read only on the publisher page, but lack a clearly identifiable license.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-25) Such articles are typically not available for reuse.

#### Diamond/platinum OA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Diamond/platinum OA")]

See also: [Diamond open access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond_open_access "Diamond open access")

Journals that publish open access without charging authors article processing charges are sometimes referred to as diamond[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-fuchs2013-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Gaj-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:1-28) or platinum[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-30) OA. Since they do not charge either readers or authors directly, such publishers often require funding from external sources such as the sale of [advertisements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advertisements "Advertisements"), [academic institutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_institution "Academic institution"), [learned societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learned_society "Learned society"), [philanthropists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philanthropist "Philanthropist") or [government grants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_grant "Government grant").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-33) There are now over 350 platinum OA journals with [impact factors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_factors "Impact factors") over a wide variety of academic disciplines, giving most academics options for OA with no APCs.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-34) Diamond OA journals are available for most disciplines, and are usually small (<25 articles per year) and more likely to be multilingual (38%); thousands of such journals exist.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:1-28)

#### Black OA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Black OA")]

See also: [Shadow library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_library "Shadow library")

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Sci-hub_downloads.png/250px-Sci-hub_downloads.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sci-hub_downloads.png)

Download rate for articles on [Sci-Hub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sci-Hub "Sci-Hub") (black open access)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-35)

The growth of unauthorized digital copying by large-scale copyright infringement has enabled free access to [paywalled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paywall "Paywall") literature.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:17-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-37) This has been done via existing social media sites (e.g. the [#ICanHazPDF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICanHazPDF "ICanHazPDF") hashtag) as well as dedicated sites (e.g. [Sci-Hub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sci-hub "Sci-hub")).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:17-36) In some ways this is a large-scale technical implementation of pre-existing practice, whereby those with access to paywalled literature would share copies with their contacts.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-41) However, the increased ease and scale from 2010 onwards have changed how many people treat subscription publications.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-42)

### Gratis and libre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Gratis and libre")]

Main article: [Gratis versus libre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gratis_versus_libre "Gratis versus libre")

Similar to the [free content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_content "Free content") definition, the terms ['gratis' and 'libre'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gratis_versus_libre "Gratis versus libre") were used in the [Budapest Open Access Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest_Open_Access_Initiative "Budapest Open Access Initiative") definition to distinguish between free to read versus free to reuse.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Gratis_and_Libre_Open_Access-43)

Gratis open access (![Image 8: Free access icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Lock-green.svg/20px-Lock-green.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)) refers to free online access, to read, free of charge, without re-use rights.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Gratis_and_Libre_Open_Access-43)

Libre open access (![Image 9: Open access icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Open_Access_logo_PLoS_transparent.svg/20px-Open_Access_logo_PLoS_transparent.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)) also refers to free online access, to read, free of charge, plus some additional re-use rights,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Gratis_and_Libre_Open_Access-43) covering the kinds of open access defined in the [Budapest Open Access Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest_Open_Access_Initiative "Budapest Open Access Initiative"), the [Bethesda Statement on Open Access Publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethesda_Statement_on_Open_Access_Publishing "Bethesda Statement on Open Access Publishing") and the [Berlin Declaration on Open Access to Knowledge in the Sciences and Humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Declaration_on_Open_Access_to_Knowledge_in_the_Sciences_and_Humanities "Berlin Declaration on Open Access to Knowledge in the Sciences and Humanities"). The re-use rights of libre OA are often specified by various specific [Creative Commons licenses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Commons_license "Creative Commons license");[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Suber_2012_68%E2%80%9369-44) all of which require as a minimum [attribution of authorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attribution_(copyright) "Attribution (copyright)") to the original authors.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Gratis_and_Libre_Open_Access-43)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Suber_statements-45) In 2012, the number of works under libre open access was considered to have been rapidly increasing for a few years, though most [open-access mandates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-access_mandate "Open-access mandate") did not enforce any copyright license and it was difficult to publish libre gold OA in legacy journals.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:0-2) However, there are no costs nor restrictions for green libre OA as preprints can be freely self-deposited with a free license, and most open-access repositories use [Creative Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Commons "Creative Commons") licenses to allow reuse.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-46)

### FAIR

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: FAIR")]

Main article: [FAIR data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FAIR_data "FAIR data")

[FAIR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FAIR_data "FAIR data") is an acronym for 'findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable', intended to more clearly define what is meant by the term 'open access' and make the concept easier to discuss.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-FAIR_principles_2016-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-48) Initially proposed in March 2016, it has subsequently been endorsed by organisations such as the [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission") and the [G20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G20 "G20").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-50) Note, however, that FAIR principles include "A1.2: The protocol allows for an authentication and authorisation procedure where necessary."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-51) This means that a FAIR dataset may be either closed (restricted access) or open (no access restrictions). So, only FAIR data without access restrictions are open access.

## Features

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Features")]

The emergence of [open science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_science "Open science") or [open research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_research "Open research") has brought to light a number of controversial and hotly-debated topics.

Scholarly publishing invokes various positions and passions. For example, authors may spend hours struggling with diverse article submission systems, often converting document formatting between a multitude of journal and conference styles, and sometimes spend months waiting for peer review results. The drawn-out and often contentious societal and technological transition to Open Access and Open Science/Open Research, particularly across North America and Europe (Latin America has already widely adopted "Acceso Abierto" since before 2000[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Alperin_2015-52)) has led to increasingly entrenched positions and much debate.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-53)

The area of (open) scholarly practices increasingly sees a role for policy-makers and research funders[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Ross-Hellauer_2018-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Vincent%E2%80%90Lamarre_2016-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Union_2019-56) giving focus to issues such as career incentives, research evaluation and business models for publicly funded research. [Plan S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plan_S "Plan S") and [AmeliCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AmeliCA?action=edit&redlink=1 "AmeliCA (page does not exist)")[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-57) (Open Knowledge for Latin America) caused a wave of debate in scholarly communication in 2019 and 2020.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Johnson_2019-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-59)

### Licenses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Licenses")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/DOAJ_licenses.png/250px-DOAJ_licenses.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DOAJ_licenses.png)

Licenses used by gold and hybrid OA journals in DOAJ[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Khing_Phyo_San-60)

Subscription-based publishing typically requires [transfer of copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_transfer "Copyright transfer") from authors to the [publisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_publisher "Academic publisher") so that the latter can monetise the process via dissemination and reproduction of the work.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Matushek_2017-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Bachrach_1998-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Gadd_2003b-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Willinsky_2002-64) With OA publishing, typically authors retain copyright to their work, and [license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/License "License") its reproduction to the publisher.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Carroll_2011-65) Retention of copyright by authors can support [academic freedoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_freedom "Academic freedom") by enabling greater control of the work (e.g. for image re-use) or licensing agreements (e.g. to allow dissemination by others).[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Davies_2015-66)

The most common licenses used in open access publishing are [Creative Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Commons_license "Creative Commons license").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:2-67) The widely used CC BY license is one of the most permissive, only requiring attribution to be allowed to use the material (and allowing derivations and commercial use).[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-68) A range of more restrictive Creative Commons licenses are also used. More rarely, some of the smaller academic journals use custom open access licenses.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:2-67)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Dodds_2018-69) Some publishers (e.g. [Elsevier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsevier "Elsevier")) use "author nominal copyright" for OA articles, where the author retains copyright in name only and all rights are transferred to the publisher.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Morrison_2017-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Alperin_2017-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Frass_2013-72)

### Funding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Funding")]

Since open access publication does not charge readers, there are many financial models used to cover costs by other means.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-73) Open access can be provided by commercial publishers, who may publish open access as well as subscription-based journals, or dedicated open-access publishers such as [Public Library of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Library_of_Science "Public Library of Science") (PLOS) and [BioMed Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BioMed_Central "BioMed Central"). Another source of funding for open access can be institutional subscribers. One example is the [Subscribe to Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subscribe_to_Open "Subscribe to Open") publishing model introduced by [Annual Reviews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annual_Reviews_(publisher) "Annual Reviews (publisher)"); if the subscription revenue goal is met, the given journal's volume is published open access.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-74) The number of journals implementing this model grew from 192 in 2024 to 378 in 2025.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Naddaf-75)

Advantages and disadvantages of open access have generated considerable discussion amongst researchers, academics, librarians, university administrators, funding agencies, government officials, commercial [publishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publisher "Publisher"), editorial staff and [society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learned_society "Learned society") publishers.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-76) Reactions of existing publishers to open access journal publishing have ranged from moving with enthusiasm to a new open access business model, to experiments with providing as much free or open access as possible, to active lobbying against open access proposals. There are many publishers that started up as open access-only publishers, such as PLOS, [Hindawi Publishing Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindawi_Publishing_Corporation "Hindawi Publishing Corporation"), [Frontiers in...](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontiers_Media "Frontiers Media") journals, [MDPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MDPI "MDPI") and BioMed Central.

#### Article processing charges

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Article processing charges")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/DOAJ_APCs.png/250px-DOAJ_APCs.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DOAJ_APCs.png)

Article processing charges by gold OA journals in DOAJ[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Khing_Phyo_San-60)

See also: [Article processing charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_processing_charge "Article processing charge")

Some open access journals (under the gold, and hybrid models) generate revenue by charging publication fees in order to make the work openly available at the time of publication.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Socha-77)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-fuchs2013-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Gaj-27) The money might come from the author but more often comes from the author's [research grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_grant "Research grant") or employer.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-78) While the payments are typically incurred _per article published_ (e.g. [BMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMC_journals "BMC journals") or [PLOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PLOS "PLOS") journals), some journals apply them _per manuscript submitted_ (e.g. _[Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric\_Chemistry\_and\_Physics "Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics")_ until recently) or _per author_ (e.g. [PeerJ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PeerJ "PeerJ")).

Charges typically range from $1,000–$3,000 ($5,380 for [Nature Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_Communications "Nature Communications"))[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-GOA4-79)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Khing_Phyo_San-60)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-80) but can be under $10,[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-81) close to $5,000[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-82) or well over $10,000.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-83) APCs vary greatly depending on subject and region and are most common in scientific and medical journals (43% and 47% respectively), and lowest in arts and humanities journals (0% and 4% respectively).[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Kozak&Hartley-84) APCs can also depend on a journal's impact factor.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Bj%C3%B6rk_2015-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Lawson_2014-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Bj%C3%B6rk_2014-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Sch%C3%B6nfelder_2018-88) Some publishers (e.g. [eLife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ELife "ELife") and [Ubiquity Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubiquity_Press "Ubiquity Press")) have released estimates of their direct and indirect costs that set their APCs.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-89)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-90) Hybrid OA generally costs more than gold OA and can offer a lower quality of service.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-auto-21) A particularly controversial practice in hybrid open access journals is "[double dipping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_dipping_(publishing) "Double dipping (publishing)")", where both authors and subscribers are charged.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Open_access_double_dipping_policy-22)

By comparison, journal subscriptions equate to $3,500–$4,000 per article published by an institution, but are highly variable by publisher (and some charge page fees separately). This has led to the assessment that there is enough money "within the system" to enable full transition to OA.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Schimmer_2015-91) However, there is ongoing discussion about whether the change-over offers an opportunity to become more cost-effective or promotes more equitable participation in publication.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-TenMyths-92) Concern has been noted that increasing subscription journal prices will be mirrored by rising APCs, creating a barrier to less financially privileged authors.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Bj%C3%B6rk_2017b-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Pinfield_2015-94)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Green_2019-95)

The inherent bias of the current APC-based OA publishing perpetuates this inequality through the '[Matthew effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_effect "Matthew effect")' (the rich get richer, and the poor get poorer). The switch from pay-to-read to pay-to-publish has left essentially the same people behind, with some academics not having enough purchasing power (individually or through their institutions) for either option.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-96) Some gold OA publishers will waive all or part of the fee for authors from [less developed economies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developing_country "Developing country"). Steps are normally taken to ensure that [peer reviewers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer_review "Peer review") do not know whether authors have requested, or been granted, fee waivers, or to ensure that every paper is approved by an independent editor with no financial stake in the journal.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The main argument against requiring authors to pay a fee, is the risk to the peer review system, diminishing the overall quality of scientific journal publishing.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

#### Subsidized or no-fee

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Subsidized or no-fee")]

No-fee open access journals, also known as "platinum" or "diamond"[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-fuchs2013-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Gaj-27) do not charge either readers or authors.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-97) These journals use a variety of [business models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_model "Business model") including subsidies, advertising, membership dues, endowments, or volunteer labour.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:3-98)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-TenMyths-92) Subsidising sources range from universities, libraries and museums to foundations, [societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learned_society "Learned society") or government agencies.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:3-98) Some publishers may cross-subsidise from other publications or auxiliary services and products.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:3-98) For example, most APC-free journals in Latin America are funded by higher education institutions and are not conditional on institutional affiliation for publication.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-TenMyths-92) Conversely, [Knowledge Unlatched](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_Unlatched "Knowledge Unlatched") crowdsources funding in order to make monographs available open access.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Montgomery-99)

Estimates of prevalence vary, but approximately 10,000 journals without APC are listed in DOAJ[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-100) and the [Free Journal Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Journal_Network "Free Journal Network").[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-101)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-102) APC-free journals tend to be smaller and more local-regional in scope.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:4-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-104) Some also require submitting authors to have a particular institutional affiliation.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:4-103)

### Preprint use

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Preprint use")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Preprint_postprint_published.svg/250px-Preprint_postprint_published.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Preprint_postprint_published.svg)

Typical publishing workflow for an academic journal article ([preprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preprint "Preprint"), [postprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postprint "Postprint"), and [published](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Version_of_record "Version of record")) with open access sharing rights per [SHERPA/RoMEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHERPA/RoMEO "SHERPA/RoMEO")

A "[preprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preprint "Preprint")" is typically a version of a research paper that is shared on an online platform prior to, or during, a formal peer review process.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Ginsparg_2016-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Tennant_2018b-106)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Neylon_2017-107) Preprint platforms have become popular due to the increasing drive towards open access publishing and can be publisher- or community-led. A range of discipline-specific or cross-domain platforms now exist.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Balaji_2019-108) The posting of pre-prints (or authors' manuscript versions) is consistent with the Green Open Access model.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

#### Effect of preprints on later publication

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Effect of preprints on later publication")]

A persistent concern surrounding preprints is that work may be at risk of being plagiarised or "scooped" – meaning that the same or similar research will be published by others without proper attribution to the original source – if publicly available but not yet associated with a stamp of approval from peer reviewers and traditional journals.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Bourne_2017-109) These concerns are often amplified as competition increases for academic jobs and funding, and perceived to be particularly problematic for early-career researchers and other higher-risk demographics within academia.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

However, preprints, in fact, protect against scooping.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Sarabipour_2019b-110) Considering the differences between traditional peer-review based publishing models and deposition of an article on a preprint server, "scooping" is less likely for manuscripts first submitted as preprints. In a traditional publishing scenario, the time from manuscript submission to acceptance and to final publication can range from a few weeks to years, and go through several rounds of revision and resubmission before final publication.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Powell_2016-111) During this time, the same work will have been extensively discussed with external collaborators, presented at conferences, and been read by editors and reviewers in related areas of research. Yet, there is no official open record of that process (e.g., peer reviewers are normally anonymous, reports remain largely unpublished), and if an identical or very similar paper were to be published while the original was still under review, it would be impossible to establish provenance.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Preprints provide a time-stamp at the time of publication, which helps to establish the "priority of discovery" for scientific claims.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-112) This means that a preprint can act as proof of provenance for research ideas, data, code, models, and results.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Crick_2017-113) The fact that the majority of preprints come with a form of permanent identifier, usually a [digital object identifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_object_identifier "Digital object identifier") (DOI), also makes them easy to cite and track. Thus, if one were to be "scooped" without adequate acknowledgement, this would be a case of academic misconduct and plagiarism, and could be pursued as such.

There is no evidence that "scooping" of research via preprints exists, not even in communities that have broadly adopted the use of the [arXiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ArXiv "ArXiv") server for sharing preprints since 1991. If the unlikely case of scooping emerges as the growth of the preprint system continues, it can be dealt with as academic malpractice. [ASAPbio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASAPbio "ASAPbio") includes a series of hypothetical scooping scenarios as part of its preprint FAQ, finding that the overall benefits of using preprints vastly outweigh any potential issues around scooping.[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-114) Indeed, the benefits of preprints, especially for early-career researchers, seem to outweigh any perceived risk: rapid sharing of academic research, open access without author-facing charges, establishing priority of discoveries, receiving wider feedback in parallel with or before peer review, and facilitating wider collaborations.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Sarabipour_2019b-110)

### Archiving

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Archiving")]

The "green" route to OA refers to author self-archiving, in which a version of the article (often the peer-reviewed version before editorial typesetting, called "postprint") is posted online to an institutional or subject repository. This route is often dependent on journal or publisher policies,[[note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-115) which can be more restrictive and complicated than respective "gold" policies regarding deposit location, license, and embargo requirements. Some publishers require an embargo period before deposition in public repositories,[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Gadd_2019-116) arguing that immediate self-archiving risks loss of subscription income. Where initial open access publishing may not be possible, academics and researchers could deposit their work in institutional and disciplinary repositories, where possible, to allow broad access to their outputs[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-117).

#### Embargo periods

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Embargo periods")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Elsevier_Embargo_lengths.png/250px-Elsevier_Embargo_lengths.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Elsevier_Embargo_lengths.png)

Length of embargo times for bronze [Elsevier journals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsevier "Elsevier")[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-118)

[Embargoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embargo_(academic_publishing) "Embargo (academic publishing)") are imposed by between 20 and 40% of journals,[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-119)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-120) during which time an article is paywalled before permitting self-archiving (green OA) or releasing a free-to-read version (bronze OA).[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-121)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-122) Embargo periods typically vary from 6–12 months in [STEM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science,_technology,_engineering,_and_mathematics "Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics") and >12 months in [humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanities "Humanities"), [arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_arts "The arts") and [social sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_sciences "Social sciences").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-TenMyths-92) Embargo-free [self-archiving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-archiving "Self-archiving") has not been shown to affect [subscription revenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subscription_business_model "Subscription business model"),[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Swan_2005-123) and tends to increase readership and citations.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-124)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-125) Embargoes have been lifted on particular topics for either limited times or ongoing (e.g. Zika outbreaks[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-126) or indigenous health[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:16-127)). [Plan S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plan_S "Plan S") includes zero-length embargoes on self-archiving as a key principle.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-TenMyths-92)

## Motivations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Motivations")]

Main article: [Academic journal publishing reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal_publishing_reform "Academic journal publishing reform")

Open access (mostly green and gratis) began to be sought and provided worldwide by researchers when the possibility itself was opened by the advent of [Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet "Internet") and the [World Wide Web](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web "World Wide Web"). The momentum was further increased by a growing movement for academic journal publishing reform, and with it gold and libre OA.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The premises behind open access publishing are that there are viable funding models to maintain traditional [peer review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer_review "Peer review") standards of quality while also making the following changes:

*   Rather than making journal articles accessible through a [subscription business model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subscription_business_model "Subscription business model"), all academic publications could be made free to read and published with some other cost-recovery model, such as publication charges, subsidies, or charging subscriptions only for the print edition, with the online edition [gratis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gratis_versus_libre "Gratis versus libre") or "free to read".[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Suber29-43-128)
*   Rather than applying traditional notions of [copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright "Copyright") to academic publications, they could be [libre](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/libre#Adjective "wikt:libre") or "free to build upon".[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Suber29-43-128)

An obvious advantage of open access journals is the free access to scientific papers regardless of affiliation with a subscribing library and improved access for the general public; this is especially true in developing countries. Lower costs for research in academia and industry have been claimed in the [Budapest Open Access Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest_Open_Access_Initiative "Budapest Open Access Initiative"),[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-129) although others have argued that OA may raise the total cost of publication,[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-130) and further increase economic incentives for exploitation in academic publishing.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-131) The open access movement is motivated by the problems of social inequality caused by restricting access to academic research, which favor large and wealthy institutions with the financial means to purchase access to many journals, as well as the economic challenges and perceived unsustainability of academic publishing.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Suber29-43-128)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-132)

### Stakeholders and concerned communities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Stakeholders and concerned communities")]

[Video 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2e/Thank_you_for_practicing_Open_Science_-_Igsi8c4BjI8.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

A fictional thank you note from the future to contemporary researchers for sharing their research openly

The intended audience of research articles is usually other researchers. Open access helps researchers as readers by opening up access to articles that their libraries do not subscribe to. All researchers benefit from open access as no library can afford to subscribe to every [scientific journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_journal "Scientific journal") and most can only afford a small fraction of them. This is known as the "[serials crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serials_crisis "Serials crisis")".[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-133)

Open access extends the reach of research beyond its immediate academic circle, as an open access article can be read by anyone. A 2008 study revealed that [mental health professionals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mental_health_professional "Mental health professional") are roughly twice as likely to read a relevant article if it is freely available.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-134)

#### Research funders

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Research funders")]

See also: §Policies and mandates

Further information: [Open-access mandate §Instances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-access_mandate#Instances "Open-access mandate")

[Research funding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_funding "Research funding") agencies and universities want to ensure that the research they fund and support in various ways has the greatest possible research impact.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-135) As a means of achieving this, research funders are beginning to expect open access to the research they support. Many of them (including all UK Research Councils) have already adopted [open-access mandates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-access_mandate "Open-access mandate"), and others are on the way to do so (see [ROARMAP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ROARMAP "ROARMAP")).

#### Universities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Universities")]

A growing number of universities are providing institutional repositories in which their researchers can deposit their published articles. Some open access advocates believe that institutional repositories will play a very important role in responding to open-access mandates from funders.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-136)

In May 2005, 16 major [Dutch universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_universities "Dutch universities") cooperatively launched [DAREnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darenet "Darenet"), the Digital Academic Repositories, making over 47,000 research papers available.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-137) From 2 June 2008, DAREnet has been incorporated into the scholarly portal [NARCIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NARCIS_(National_Academic_Research_and_Collaboration_Information_System) "NARCIS (National Academic Research and Collaboration Information System)").[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-138) By 2019, NARCIS provided access to 360,000 open access publications from all Dutch universities, [KNAW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Netherlands_Academy_of_Arts_and_Sciences "Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences"), [NWO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_Organisation_for_Scientific_Research "Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research") and a number of scientific institutes.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-139)

In 2011, a group of universities in North America formed the Coalition of Open Access Policy Institutions (COAPI).[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-140) Starting with 21 institutions where the faculty had either established an open access policy or were in the process of implementing one, COAPI now has nearly 50 members. These institutions' administrators, faculty and librarians, and staff support the international work of the Coalition's awareness-raising and advocacy for open access.

In 2012, the Harvard Open Access Project released its guide to good practices for university open-access policies,[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-141) focusing on rights-retention policies that allow universities to distribute faculty research without seeking permission from publishers. As of November 2023, Rights retention policies are being adopted by an increasing number of UK universities as well.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 2013 a group of nine Australian universities formed the Australian Open Access Strategy Group (AOASG) to advocate, collaborate, raise awareness, and lead and build capacity in the open access space in Australia.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-142) In 2015, the group expanded to include all eight New Zealand universities and was renamed the Australasian Open Access Support Group.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-143) It was then renamed the Australasian Open Access Strategy Group, highlighting its emphasis on strategy. The awareness raising activities of the AOASG include presentations, workshops, blogs, and a webinar series on open access issues.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-144)

#### Libraries and librarians

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Libraries and librarians")]

As information professionals, [librarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Librarian "Librarian") are often vocal and active advocates of open access. These librarians believe that open access promises to remove both the price and permission barriers that undermine library efforts to provide access to scholarship, as well as helping to address the [serials crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serials_crisis "Serials crisis").[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-145) Open access provides a complement to library access services such as [interlibrary loan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interlibrary_loan "Interlibrary loan"), supporting researchers' needs for immediate access to scholarship.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-146) Librarians and library associations also lead education and outreach initiatives to faculty, administrators, the library community, and the public about the benefits of open access.

Many library associations have either signed major open access declarations or created their own. For example, [IFLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_of_Library_Associations_and_Institutions "International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions") have produced a Statement on Open Access.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-147) The [Association of Research Libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Research_Libraries "Association of Research Libraries") has documented the need for increased access to scholarly information, and was a leading founder of the [Scholarly Publishing and Academic Resources Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholarly_Publishing_and_Academic_Resources_Coalition "Scholarly Publishing and Academic Resources Coalition") (SPARC).[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-148)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-149) Librarians and library associations also develop and share informational resources on scholarly publishing and open access to research; the Scholarly Communications Toolkit[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-150) developed by the [Association of College and Research Libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_College_and_Research_Libraries "Association of College and Research Libraries") of the [American Library Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Library_Association "American Library Association") is one example of this work.

At most universities, the library manages the institutional repository, which provides free access to scholarly work by the university's faculty. The [Canadian Association of Research Libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Association_of_Research_Libraries "Canadian Association of Research Libraries") has a program[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-151) to develop institutional repositories at all Canadian university libraries. An increasing number of libraries provide [publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_publishing "Library publishing") or hosting services for open access journals, with the Library Publishing Coalition as a membership organisation.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-152)

In 2013, open access activist [Aaron Swartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Swartz "Aaron Swartz") was posthumously awarded the American Library Association's [James Madison Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Madison_Award "James Madison Award") for being an "outspoken advocate for public participation in government and unrestricted access to peer-reviewed scholarly articles".[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-153)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-154) In March 2013, the entire editorial board and the editor-in-chief of the _[Journal of Library Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal\_of\_Library\_Administration "Journal of Library Administration")_ resigned en masse, citing a dispute with the journal's publisher.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-155) One board member wrote of a "crisis of conscience about publishing in a journal that was not open access" after the death of Aaron Swartz.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-156)[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-157)

#### Public

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Public")]

The public may benefit from open access to scholarly research for many reasons. Advocacy groups such as [SPARC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholarly_Publishing_and_Academic_Resources_Coalition "Scholarly Publishing and Academic Resources Coalition")'s Alliance for Taxpayer Access in the US argue that most scientific research is paid for by taxpayers through [government grants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_grant "Government grant"), who have a right to access the results of what they have funded.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-158) Examples of people who might wish to read scholarly literature include individuals with medical conditions and their family members, serious hobbyists or "amateur" scholars (e.g. [amateur astronomers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_astronomy "Amateur astronomy")), and high school and [junior college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_college "Junior college") students. Additionally, professionals in many fields, such as those doing research in private companies, [start-ups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Start-up "Start-up"), and hospitals, may not have access to publications behind paywalls, and OA publications are the only type that they can access in practice.

Even those who do not read scholarly articles benefit indirectly from open access.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-159) For example, patients benefit when their doctor and other [health care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_care "Health care") professionals have access to the latest research. Advocates argue that open access speeds research progress, productivity, and knowledge translation.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-160)

#### Low-income countries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Low-income countries")]

In developing nations, open access archiving and publishing acquires a unique importance.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-161) Scientists, health care professionals, and institutions in developing nations often do not have the capital necessary to access scholarly literature.

Many open access projects involve international collaboration. For example, the [SciELO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SciELO "SciELO") (Scientific Electronic Library Online),[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-162) is a comprehensive approach to full open access journal publishing, involving a number of [Latin American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America") countries. [Bioline International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioline_International "Bioline International"), a [non-profit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit_organization "Non-profit organization") dedicated to helping publishers in developing countries is a collaboration of people in the UK, Canada, and Brazil; the Bioline International Software is used around the world. [Research Papers in Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Papers_in_Economics "Research Papers in Economics") (RePEc), is a collaborative effort of over 100 volunteers in 45 countries. The [Public Knowledge Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Knowledge_Project "Public Knowledge Project") in Canada developed the [open-source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-source_software "Open-source software") publishing software [Open Journal Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Journal_Systems "Open Journal Systems") (OJS), which is now in use around the world, for example by the [African Journals Online](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Journals_Online "African Journals Online") group, and one of the most active development groups is Portuguese. This international perspective has resulted in advocacy for the development of [open-source appropriate technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-source_appropriate_technology "Open-source appropriate technology") and the necessary open access to relevant information for [sustainable development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_development "Sustainable development").[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-163)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-164)

### Extent

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Extent")]

Various studies have investigated the extent of open access. A study published in 2010 showed that roughly 20% of the total number of peer-reviewed articles published in 2008 could be found openly accessible.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-doi10.1371/journal.pone.0011273-166) Another study found that by 2010, 7.9% of all academic journals with [impact factors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_factor "Impact factor") were gold open access journals and showed a broad distribution of Gold Open Access journals throughout academic disciplines.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-167) A study of random journals from the [citations indexes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_index "Citation index") AHSCI, SCI and SSCI in 2013 came to the result that 88% of the journals were closed access and 12% were open access.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-fuchs2013-26) In August 2013, a study done for the [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission") reported that 50% of a random sample of all articles published in 2011 as indexed by [Scopus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopus "Scopus") were freely accessible online by the end of 2012.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-168)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-169)[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-170) A 2017 study by the [Max Planck Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Planck_Society "Max Planck Society") put the share of gold access articles in pure open access journals at around 13 percent of total research papers.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Max_Planck_Gesellschaft-171)

In 2009, there were approximately 4,800 active open access journals, publishing around 190,000 articles.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Bj%C3%B6rk2011-172) As of February 2019, over 12,500 open access journals are listed in the [Directory of Open Access Journals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directory_of_Open_Access_Journals "Directory of Open Access Journals").[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Directory_of_Open_Access_Journals-173)

Note: articles may be both green and gold OA so x and y values do not sum to total OA.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-174)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-175)

A 2013-2018 report (GOA4) found that in 2018 over 700,000 articles were published in gold open access in the world, of which 42% was in journals with no author-paid fees.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-GOA4-79) The figure varies significantly depending on region and kind of publisher: 75% if university-run, over 80% in Latin America, but less than 25% in Western Europe.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-GOA4-79) However, Crawford's study did not count open access articles published in "hybrid" journals (subscription journals that allow authors to make their individual articles open in return for payment of a fee). More comprehensive analyses of the scholarly literature suggest that this resulted in a significant underestimation of the prevalence of author-fee-funded OA publications in the literature.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-176) Crawford's study also found that although a minority of open access _journals_ impose charges on authors, a growing majority of open access _articles_ are published under this arrangement, particularly in the science disciplines (thanks to the enormous output of open access "mega journals", each of which may publish tens of thousands of articles in a year and are invariably funded by author-side charges—see Figure 10.1 in GOA4).

According to [Scopus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scopus "Scopus") database in August, 2024, 46.2% of works, indexed therein and published in 2023, had some form of open access. More than half of the OA publications (27.5% of all indexed works in 2023) were in fully Gold Open Access sources, 16.7% of all were in Green OA sources (i.e. which allow for self-archiving by authors), 9.2% in Hybrid Gold OA sources (such as journals, which have open access and behind-paywall articles in the same issue), and 10.6% were in Bronze OA sources (free-to-read on the publishers' websites).[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-177)
