The adoption of Open Access publishing varies significantly from publisher to publisher, as shown in Fig. OA-Plot, where only the oldest (traditional) publishers are shown, but not the newer publishers, that use the Open Access model exclusively. This plot shows, that since 2010 the [Institute of Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Physics "Institute of Physics") has the largest percentage of OA publications, while the [American Chemical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Chemical_Society "American Chemical Society") has the lowest. Both the IOP and the ACS are non-profit publishers. The increase in OA percentage for articles published before ca. 1923 is related to the expiration of a 100-year [copyright term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_term "Copyright term"). Some publishers (e.g. IOP and ACS made many such articles available as Open Access, while others ([Elsevier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elsevier "Elsevier") in particular) did not.

The [Registry of Open Access Repositories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Registry_of_Open_Access_Repositories "Registry of Open Access Repositories") (ROAR) indexes the creation, location and growth of open access [open access-repositories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-access_repository "Open-access repository") and their contents.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-roar2-178) As of February 2019, over 4,500 institutional and cross-institutional repositories have been registered in ROAR.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-179)

## Effects on scholarly publishing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Effects on scholarly publishing")]

### Article impact

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Article impact")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Open_access_citation_advantage.png/250px-Open_access_citation_advantage.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Open_access_citation_advantage.png)

Comparison of OA publications to non-OA publications for academic citations (n=44),[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-mckiernan-180) HTML views (n=4),[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:10-181)[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:12-182)[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:13-183)[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:14-184) PDF downloads (n=3),[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:12-182)[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:13-183)[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:14-184) Twitter (n=2),[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:6-185)[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:10-181) Wikipedia (n=1)[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:8-186)

Since published articles report on research that is typically funded by government or university grants, the more the article is used, cited, applied and built upon, the better for research as well as for the researcher's career.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-uk-187)[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-188)

Some professional organizations have encouraged use of open access: in 2001, the [International Mathematical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Mathematical_Union "International Mathematical Union") communicated to its members that "Open access to the mathematical literature is an important goal" and encouraged them to "[make] available electronically as much of our own work as feasible" to "[enlarge] the reservoir of freely available primary mathematical material, particularly helping scientists working without adequate library access".[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-imu-189)

#### Readership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Readership")]

OA articles are generally viewed online and downloaded more often than paywalled articles and that readership continues for longer.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:10-181)[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:9-190) Readership is especially higher in demographics that typically lack access to subscription journals (in addition to the general population, this includes many medical practitioners, patient groups, policymakers, non-profit sector workers, industry researchers, and independent researchers).[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:5-191) OA articles are more read on publication management programs such as Mendeley.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:6-185) Open access practices can reduce publication delays, an obstacle which led some research fields such as high-energy physics to adopt widespread preprint access.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-192)

#### Citation rate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Citation rate")]

See also: [FUTON bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FUTON_bias "FUTON bias")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Open_access_addendum_for_authors_to_publishers.pdf/page1-250px-Open_access_addendum_for_authors_to_publishers.pdf.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Open_access_addendum_for_authors_to_publishers.pdf)

Authors may use form language like this to request an open access license when submitting their work to a publisher.

[Video 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b7/How_Open_Access_Empowered_a_16-Year-Old_to_Make_Cancer_Breakthrough.ogv?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=index&utm_content=original)

A 2013 interview on [paywalls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paywall "Paywall") and open access with [NIH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health") Director [Francis Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Collins "Francis Collins") and inventor [Jack Andraka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Andraka "Jack Andraka")

A main reason authors make their articles openly accessible is to maximize their [citation impact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_impact "Citation impact").[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-193) Open access articles are typically [cited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation "Citation") more often than equivalent articles requiring subscriptions.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:0-2)[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-194)[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-195)[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:7-196)[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:11-197) This 'citation advantage' was first reported in 2001.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-198) Although two major studies dispute this claim,[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Davis_2008-199)[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:9-190) the consensus of multiple studies support the effect,[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-mckiernan-180)[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-autogenerated3-200) with measured OA citation advantage varying in magnitude between 1.3-fold to 6-fold depending on discipline.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:7-196)[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-201)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Clayson_103%E2%80%93111-202)

Citation advantage is most pronounced in OA articles in hybrid journals (compared to the non-OA articles in those same journals),[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-203) and with articles deposited in green OA repositories.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-doi10.1371/journal.pone.0011273-166) Notably, green OA articles show similar benefits to citation counts as gold OA articles.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Clayson_103%E2%80%93111-202)[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:11-197) Articles in gold OA journals are typically cited at a similar frequency to paywalled articles.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-204) Citation advantage increases the longer an article has been published.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:10-181) A 2024 article demonstrated that open-access (OA) publications receive more diverse citations than closed-access publications, in terms of institutions, countries, subregions, regions, and research fields. This citation diversity advantage is robust, as observed across 19 million publications and 420 million citations (2010–2019). Analysis of the extant literature indicates that open access through disciplinary or institutional repositories showed a stronger effect than open access via publisher platforms.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-205)

#### Altmetrics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Altmetrics")]

In addition to format academic [citation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation "Citation"), other forms of research impact ([altmetrics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altmetrics "Altmetrics")) may be affected by OA publishing,[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:5-191)[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:11-197) constituting a significant "amplifier" effect for science published on such platforms.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:8-186) Initial studies suggest that OA articles are more referenced in blogs,[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-206) on Twitter,[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:6-185) and on English Wikipedia.[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:8-186)[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-207) The OA advantage in altmetrics may be smaller than the advantage in academic citations, although findings are mixed.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-208)[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:11-197)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Clayson_103%E2%80%93111-202)

### Journal impact factor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=34 "Edit section: Journal impact factor")]

See also: [Impact factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_factor "Impact factor")

[Journal impact factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_impact_factor "Journal impact factor") (JIF) measures the average number of citations of articles in a journal over a two-year window. It is commonly used as a proxy for journal quality, expected research impact for articles submitted to that journal, and of researcher success.[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Lariviere_2018-209)[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Curry_2018-210) In subscription journals, impact factor correlates with overall citation count, however this correlation is not observed in gold OA journals.[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-211)

Open access initiatives like [Plan S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plan_S "Plan S") typically call on a broader adoption and implementation of the [Leiden Manifesto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leiden_Manifesto "Leiden Manifesto")[[note 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-212) and the [San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Declaration_on_Research_Assessment "San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment") (DORA) alongside fundamental changes in the scholarly communication system.[[note 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-213)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=35 "Edit section: Peer review processes")]

practices.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Munaf%C3%B2_2017b-224)[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Bowman_2018-225)[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-McKiernan_2016-226) It is proposed that increased transparency of academic quality control processes makes audit of the academic record easier.[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:15-221)[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-227) Additionally, the rise of OA ### Predatory publishing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: Predatory publishing")]

[Predatory publishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predatory_publishing "Predatory publishing") present themselves as academic journals but use lax or no peer review processes coupled with aggressive advertising in order to generate revenue from article processing charges from authors. The definitions of 'predatory', 'deceptive', or 'questionable' publishers/journals are often vague, opaque, and confusing, and can also include fully legitimate journals, such as those indexed by PubMed Central.[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-230) In this sense, Grudniewicz et al.[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-231) proposed a consensus definition that needs to be shared: "Predatory journals and publishers are entities that prioritize self-interest at the expense of scholarship and are characterized by false or misleading information, deviation from best editorial and publication practices, a lack of transparency, and/or the use of aggressive and indiscriminate solicitation practices."

In this way, predatory journals exploit the OA model by deceptively removing the main value added by the journal (peer review) and parasitize the OA movement, occasionally hijacking or impersonating other journals.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-232)[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-233) The rise of such journals since 2010[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Shen_2015-234)[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Perlin_2018-235) has damaged the reputation of the OA publishing model as a whole, especially via sting operations where fake papers have been successfully published in such journals.[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Bohannon_2013-236) Although commonly associated with OA publishing models, subscription journals are also at risk of similar lax quality control standards and poor editorial policies.[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Olivarez_2018-237)[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Shamseer_2017-238)[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-239) OA publishers therefore aim to ensure quality via auditing by registries such as [DOAJ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOAJ "DOAJ"), [OASPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Access_Scholarly_Publishing_Association "Open Access Scholarly Publishing Association") and [SciELO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SciELO "SciELO") and comply to a standardised set of conditions. A blacklist of predatory publishers is also maintained by [Cabell's blacklist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabell's_blacklist "Cabell's blacklist") (a successor to [Beall's List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beall's_List "Beall's List")).[[236]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Silver_2017-240)[[237]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Strinzel_2019-241) Increased transparency of the peer review and publication process has been proposed as a way to combat predatory journal practices.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-TenMyths-92)[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-:15-221)[[238]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Polka_2018-242)

### Open irony

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: Open irony")]

Open irony refers to the situation where a scholarly journal article advocates open access but the article itself is only accessible by paying a fee to the journal publisher to read the article.[[239]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-243)[[240]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-244)[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Open_Access_to_Publications_to_Expa-245) This has been noted in many fields, with more than 20 examples appearing since around 2010, including in widely-read journals such as _[The Lancet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lancet "The Lancet")_, _[Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science\_(journal) "Science (journal)")_ and _[Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature\_(journal) "Nature (journal)")_. In 2012 Duncan Hull proposed the Open Access Irony award to publicly humiliate journals that publish these kinds of papers.[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-246) Examples of these have been shared and discussed on social media using the [hashtag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashtag "Hashtag") #openirony. Typically, these discussions are humorous exposures of articles/editorials that are pro-open access, but locked behind paywalls. The main concern that motivates these discussions is that restricted access to public scientific knowledge is slowing scientific progress.[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Open_Access_to_Publications_to_Expa-245) The practice has been justified as important for raising awareness of open access.[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-247)

### Databases and repositories

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Open_access&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: Databases and repositories")]

Multiple databases exist for open access articles, journals and datasets. These databases overlap, however each has different inclusion criteria, which typically include extensive vetting for journal publication practices, editorial boards and ethics statements. The main databases of open access articles and journals are [DOAJ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOAJ "DOAJ") and [PMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PubMed_Central "PubMed Central"). In the case of DOAJ, only fully gold open access journals are included, whereas PMC also hosts articles from hybrid journals. Openaccess.CC is also a community based repository that maintain the database of active journals and articles.[[245]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-249)

There are also a number of [preprint servers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preprint_server "Preprint server") which host articles that have not yet been reviewed as open access copies.[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-250)[[247]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-251) These articles are subsequently submitted for peer review by both open access and subscription journals, however the preprint always remains openly accessible. A list of preprint servers is maintained at ResearchPreprints.[[248]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-252)

For articles that are published in closed access journals, some authors will deposit a postprint copy in an [open-access repository](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-access_repository "Open-access repository"), where it can be accessed for free.[[249]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-253)[[250]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-254)[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-greenandgold2-255)[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-roar2-178)[[252]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-DemystifyingOpenAccess2-256) Most subscription journals place restrictions on which version of the work may be shared or require an [embargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embargo_(academic_publishing) "Embargo (academic publishing)") period following the original date of publication. What is deposited can therefore vary, either a [preprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preprint "Preprint") or the peer-reviewed [postprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postprint "Postprint"), either the author's refereed and revised final draft or the publisher's [version of record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Version_of_record "Version of record"), either immediately deposited or after several years.[[253]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-Embargos2-257) Repositories may be specific to an [institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institutional_repository "Institutional repository"), a [discipline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disciplinary_repository "Disciplinary repository") (e.g.[arXiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ArXiv "ArXiv")), a [scholarly society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholarly_society "Scholarly society") (e.g. [MLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Language_Association "Modern Language Association")'s CORE Repository), or a funder (e.g. PMC). Although the practice was first formally proposed in 1994,[[254]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-258)[[255]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-259) self-archiving was already being practiced by some computer scientists in local [FTP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FTP "FTP") archives in the 1980s (later harvested by [CiteSeer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CiteSeer "CiteSeer")).[[256]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-260) The [SHERPA/RoMEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHERPA/RoMEO "SHERPA/RoMEO") site maintains a list of the different publisher copyright and self-archiving policies[[257]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-261) and the [ROAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ROAR_Registry_of_Open_Access_Repositories "ROAR Registry of Open Access Repositories") database hosts an index of the repositories themselves.[[258]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-262)[[259]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_access#cite_note-263)[_[check quotation syntax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style#Punctuation "Wikipedia:Manual of Style")_]

## Abstract

Vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency (VDD) is a very prevalent condition in the general population. Vitamin D is necessary for optimal bone mineralization, but apart from the bone effects, preclinical and observational studies have suggested that vitamin D may have pleiotropic actions, whereas VDD has been linked to several diseases and higher all-cause mortality. Thus, supplementing vitamin D has been considered a safe and inexpensive approach to generate better health outcomes—and especially so in frail populations. Whereas it is generally accepted that prescribing of vitamin D in VDD subjects has demonstrable health benefits, most randomized clinical trials, although with design constraints, assessing the effects of vitamin D supplementation on a variety of diseases have failed to demonstrate any positive effects of vitamin D supplementation. In this narrative review, we first describe mechanisms through which vitamin D may exert an important role in the pathophysiology of the discussed disorder, and then provide studies that have addressed the impact of VDD and of vitamin D supplementation on each disorder, focusing especially on randomized clinical trials and meta-analyses. Despite there already being vast literature on the pleiotropic actions of vitamin D, future research approaches that consider and circumvent the inherent difficulties in studying the effects of vitamin D supplementation on health outcomes are needed to assess the potential beneficial effects of vitamin D. The evaluation of the whole vitamin D endocrine system, rather than only of 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels before and after treatment, use of adequate and physiologic vitamin D dosing, grouping based on the achieved vitamin D levels rather than the amount of vitamin D supplementation subjects may receive, and sufficiently long follow-up are some of the aspects that need to be carefully considered in future studies.

## Introduction

Vitamin D insufficiency or deficiency (VDD) have been identified as very prevalent conditions in the general population, with some authors coining the use of the terms of “vitamin D deficiency epidemic, or pandemic” [1, 2]. Other than the well-known effects of vitamin D on bone metabolism, vitamin D exerts pleiotropic actions. On one hand, VDD is associated with a series of adverse health conditions; on the other, supplementation with vitamin D is a low‐cost and safe intervention, making it an attractive therapeutic option in the clinician’s and researcher’s armature. These facts have contributed to the “explosion” in the interest of the scientific community on the understanding of the pleiotropic actions of vitamin D, among which is its immunomodulating effects.

Currently, there is vast research on the effects of vitamin D on human homeostasis, mechanisms of action, and supplementation outcomes. Up to June 2022, a PUBMED (MeSH) search on vitamin D yielded 65,758 results, with abrupt increases in the scientific publications in the last two decades. However, many of the published studies that have linked decreased vitamin D levels with poorer health outcomes are of associative nature, making the evidence whether vitamin D per se contributes or not to poor health relatively weak. In this narrative review, we present the links between VDD and a variety of diseases such as infections, COVID-19, type 2 diabetes (T2D), hypertension, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, neurodegenerative and autoimmune diseases, and also the impact of vitamin D supplementation. First, we describe briefly, the mechanisms through which vitamin D could have an impact on the discussed pathology (Fig. 1). Then, we provide the available evidence from purely an association point of view. Since association does not prove causation, and there are often undetected confounders in reported associations, we then focused on meta-analyses and systematic reviews where vitamin D administration has been tested in the treatment or prognosis of the disease in question. Original articles and/or meta-analyses on the supplementation of vitamin D outcomes are also provided if available.Fig. 1Mechanisms through which vitamin D may impact on bone health, immunity, cancer, cardiovascular disease, and neuroprotection

### Regulation of Vitamin D

Vitamin D exists in two major forms: vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol) and vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol); the former is obtained with diet mainly from fungi and also plants, whereas the latter can be either obtained with diet (animal products) or synthesized in the skin from the conversion of the cholesterol precursor 7-dehydrocholesterol after exposure to adequate ultraviolet B radiation. Sun exposure for vitamin D synthesis may be efficient only when the angle of sun rays is more than 45°. As a result of this, inhabitants of the northern hemisphere do not receive sufficient amounts of vitamin D through skin synthesis during winter months, and in some northern areas, defective sun exposure may last up to 6 months of the year [3]. Moreover, a typical Western diet is poor in vitamin D [4]. To increase vitamin D ingestion, some countries have applied a policy of enriching milk products [5, 6] and margarine [7] with vitamin D, while also the use of light bulbs for artificial UVB exposure is another tool to increase vitamin D synthesis.

Vitamin D needs to undergo activation, which consists of two consecutive hydroxylations; the first in the liver and the second predominantly in the kidneys, but also in extrarenal tissues. In the liver, cholecalciferol is quickly hydroxylated by the enzyme 25-hydroxylase (a CYP450-dependent enzyme also known as CYP2R1) yielding 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) in an uncontrolled process [8]. Low plasma calcium or phosphate levels regulate parathyroid hormone (PTH) and fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF-23) levels, leading to the 1α-hydroxylation of 25(OH)D in the kidney and particularly in the mitochondria of the proximal convoluted tubule cells by the 1-hydroxylase enzyme (CYP27B1), resulting in the active vitamin D (1,25(OH)2 D) [9] (Fig. 2). The 1α-hydroxylation may also occur in extrarenal tissues (epithelial tissues, placenta, bone, endocrine glands, brain, liver, and endothelium [10, 11]), and especially in immune cells [12]. The 1,25(OH)2 D can then de-activate 1α-hydroxylase and stimulate the 24-hydroxylase enzyme, which destroys 25(OH)D, providing a negative feedback loop that controls active vitamin D levels. The 24-hydroxylation of 25(OH)D yields 24,25(OH)2 D, the inactive metabolite, the formation of which, along with saturation of the synthesis of vitamin D in the skin, guards against vitamin D intoxication. Even though the active form of vitamin D is 1,25(OH)2 D, conventional blood tests measure 25(OH)D because of its long half-life (~15 days) [13], making it a suitable marker of vitamin D storage. In contrast, circulating 1,25(OH)2 D does not reflect vitamin D status because of its short half-life of a few hours and its tight regulation by PTH, calcium, and phosphate levels [14]. The direct measurement of free (non-protein bound) 25(OH)D is also possible, with some authors proposing that the contemporaneous assessment of total and free 25(OH)D levels, as well as vitamin D binding protein (VDBP) and PTH should be measured in assessing vitamin D status and the effect of vitamin D supplementation on clinical outcomes [15–18].Fig. 2Schematic representation of 1α-hydroxylation of 25 (OH)D in the active form in renal and extrarenal tissues.
