## Highlights

• Probiotics alleviate IBD through different mechanisms of action.

• Free probiotics are easily degraded during processing and digestion.

• The delivery system enhances the biological activity of probiotics.

• Probiotics for alleviating IBD were introduced to the intestine attributed to the different probiotic delivery systems.

• Engineered probiotic delivery is a novel approach to alleviating IBD.

## Abstract

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) influences several million people around the globe, with a high prevalence in North America and Europe. Results from the studies about host-gut microbial interactions demonstrated that gut microbiota plays a critical role in the progression of IBD, and probiotics can significantly improve microflora dysbiosis and inflammatory response caused by intestinal pathogens. However, several limitations existed for the probiotics delivered to the intestine in the free form (non-encapsulated), such as low pH and diverse digestive enzymes in the gastrointestinal tract, etc. To overcome the problems, several probiotic delivery systems were established and verified with effects. Here, the types and applications of probiotics in animal models and clinical studies are first reviewed in this paper. Subsequently, various types of probiotic delivery systems are elaborated, containing the well-known microcapsules and hydrogel delivery systems, and the engineered probiotic delivery systems are also introduced. Furthermore, mechanisms of action associated with probiotics are illustrated, including maintaining gut microbiota barrier balance, modulating the immune response, and alleviating oxidative stress, etc. Finally, we discussed the relative advantages and disadvantages of different encapsulation methods, as well as future trends for further development of probiotic delivery systems with health benefits.

## 1 Introduction

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic intestinal disease known as progressive, nonspecific, and recurrent, which induces long-term inflammation of the colon and can lead to the symptoms of fever vomiting, persistent diarrhea, as well as abdominal pain. In addition, another feature of IBD is abnormal feces, which may contain blood and mucus. The IBD can be divided into two types, including Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC)[1], according to the lesion locations. The lesions of UC are mainly confined to the inflammation of rectal and colon mucosa and submucosa, showing continuous and diffuse distribution[2]; CD lesions are marked by segmental in flammation which can involve anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract, but most often involve the distal ileum[3]. Most IBD patients are between 33 and 39 years old[4], and this seriously affects their quality of life and daily life, resulting in increased medical costs. Since the 21 st century, with the rapid development of urbanization and social economy, there has been a dramatic rise in the prevalence of IBD around the world[5]. The causes of IBD are still unclear, but is widely recognized to be related to several factors, such as genetics, immune imbalance, intestinal microecological imbalance, diet, environment, and other factors[6].

Traditional drug therapies for IBD are non-targeted, and commonly used medications include aminosalicylic acid, glucocorticoids, antibiotics, corticosteroids, and immunosuppressants. These drugs inhibit inflammation by reducing the opportunities for bacterial infection of mucosal wounds[7].

It has been demonstrated that patients with IBD have changes in the intestinal microenvironment, including imbalances in the gut microbiota and increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which ultimately lead to intestinal mucosal damage[8]. A genetic catalog of the microbial species that inhabit a defined environment such as the human body is called the microbiome[9], and unlike the human genome, which is rarely altered by external intervention, intestinal microbiota compositions are readily altered through diet, pathogen infections, antibiotic intake, as well as other life events. When the balance of the human gut is out of whack, it can lead to intestinal diseases and complications. There are a variety of probiotics in the human gut microbiota, including _Lactobacillus_, _Bifidobacterium_, _Streptococcus_, etc. These probiotics can alleviate IBD and promote human health through mechanisms such as maintaining the balance of gut microbiota and regulating cytokine secretion[10]. Therefore, delivering probiotics is an effective way to alleviate IBD. However, oral (non-embedded) probiotics are easily degraded by the harsh conditions within the human gastrointestinal tract, including the low pH in the stomach, as well as the bile salts and digestive enzymes in the small intestine[11]. It is necessary to establish a targeted delivery system that protects probiotics from degradation. Here, we collected 1179 research articles focusing on probiotics and IBD from 2019 to 2023 by searching the Web of Science database, and the keyword co-occurrence network diagram shows that the probiotic delivery system for the alleviation of IBD has been widely used in mouse models, clinical double-blind trials, and other fields (Fig. 1). In addition, the research mainly focuses on probiotic species, mechanisms, and applications. Here, we focus on three probiotics (_Lactobacillus_, _Bifidobacterium_, and _Streptococcus_) that can alleviate IBD.

## 2 Therapeutic applications of probiotics in IBD

Appropriate probiotic dose administration has positive effects on host organisms. Studies showed that the probiotic species that can alleviate IBD mainly contain _Lactobacillus_, _Bifidobacterium_, _Streptococcus_, etc. (Table 1), and also include mixed probiotics. Some of these are mainly derived from yogurt, cheese, pickles, kefir, sourdough bread, fermented bean curd, tempeh, etc. These probiotics have many benefits for the body (Fig. 2). These probiotic strains are effective in alleviating IBD, either in mouse or rat disease models or in clinical studies (Tables 1 and 2). Dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) and 2,4,6-trinitrobenzene sulfonic acid (TNBS) are often used to induce colitis in animal models. DSS is mainly used to induce UC, and TNBS is widely used to induce CD[12].

## 2.1 Single probiotics applications

## 2.1.1 Lactobacillus

_Lactobacillus_ belongs to Gram-positive bacteria, which can be divided into obligate anaerobic, facultative anaerobic, or microaerophilic types[35]. At present, the common _Lactobacillus_ species include _L_. _plantarum_, _L_. _rhamnosus_, _L_. _acidophilus_, and others. Plenty of animal studies have demonstrated that these _Lactobacillus_ have effects on alleviating colitis in mice. For example, Zan et al.[16] found that _L_. _plantarum_ 6076 had a significant alleviating effect on DSS-induced colitis. It not only alters the composition of the gut microbiota but also reduces inflammation by reducing oxidative stress. This study provides novel insights into the alleviation of IBD and holds potential clinical applications. Liu et al.[17] experimentally demonstrated that _L_. _valerate_ YQ001 and _L_. _advancedus_ YQ005 were able to reduce the expression levels of pro-inflammatory factors IL-1β and IL-6 and improve the gut microbiota. This suggests that these two strains have anti-inflammatory effects, and also provide new insights and new resources for the development of food-based therapies for chronic diseases.

In children with UC, mucosal inflammation can be effectively alleviated by the administration of _L_. _reuteri_ ATCC 55730, which alters the expression levels of cytokines affecting IBD[28]. In colonic mucosa of patients with mild UC, D’Incà et al.[29] found that rectal administration of _L_. _casei_ DG modifies not only pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β and TNF-α levels decreased and anti-inflammatory factor IL-10 increased, but also improves the colonic microbiota (_Lactobacillus_ increased, Enterobacteriaceae decreased). Within the patient-based studies, Hegazy et al.[30] found that _L._ _fermentum_ not only reduced NF-κB DNA binding activity, but also reduced leukocyte accumulation and down-regulated IL-6 and TNF-α production, thereby alleviating the severity of colitis.

In general, _Lactobacillus_ shows potential as an intervention for IBD. It can modulate the immune response, reduce inflammation, etc., but further research is needed to better understand the mechanisms of beneficial effects of _Lactobacillus_ and to determine the optimal strains and dosages for use in patients with IBD clinical treatment.

## 2.1.2 Bifidobacterium

_Bifidobacterium_ belongs to Gram-positive bacteria and anaerobic type. Among them, _Bifidobacterium_ is a V-shaped or Y-shaped branch of Bifidobacteriaceae and Actinobacteria, which is distributed throughout the intestinal tract of animals and humans. It maintains intestinal microecological balance, immunomodulation, and antimicrobial activity[36]. _Bifidobacterium_, as a representative class of probiotics in the human gastrointestinal tract, not only has obvious therapeutic effects but also has the advantage of having fewer side effects, etc. _B_. _infantis_ is a type of probiotic normally found in the human gut. It can alter the balance of gut microbiota in the gastrointestinal tract, thus helping to reduce inflammation. Such as, it has been demonstrated that _B_. _infantis_ not only promotes the recovery of inflammatory tissues in the TNBS model of rat colitis but also supports the maintenance of colonic integrity against chronic inflammatory processes[18]. This shows that _B_. _infantis_ has an important role in maintaining colon morphology. Modulation of gut microbiota also gives us inspiration for preventing and alleviating IBD through dietary modifications.

_B_. _breve_ M-16V is a probiotic with a long tradition of use in neonatal intensive care units in some countries. Izumi et al.[37] induced colitis in rats with DSS and then found that _B. breve_ M-16V had a certain alleviating effect on colitis in weaned rats. Thus, this strain is considered a safe strain to use not only in neonatal infants but also in weaning children. _Bifidobacterium_ has better intestinal tolerance than other species such as _Lactobacillus_, but in some cases, embedding it can also enhance its vitality and play a better role. For example, Li et al.[38] encapsulated _B. breve_ in spherical calcium alginate (CA) beads with a smooth surface by the emulsion method and then simulated various pH environments in the gastrointestinal tract. It demonstrated a remarkable increase in the viability of the encapsulated _B. breve_. Wang et al.[39] embedded probiotics with hyaluronic acid-bilirubin nanomedicine (HABN). The synthesized BL@HABN not only reduced pro-inflammatory factors and repaired the epithelial barrier, but also restored the abundance and diversity of the intestinal microbiota.

Within the patient-based studies, Tamaki et al.[31] demonstrated in a clinical study that _B_. _longum_ 536 improved the clinical symptoms of UC patients. In addition, Groeger et al.[32] demonstrated that _B. infantis_ 35624 can reduce the levels of C-reactive protein and the pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-6 in UC patients. Although the efficacy of _Bifidobacterium_ in the alleviation of IBD is well established, further research is needed to confirm the efficacy and safety of probiotic therapy in clinical studies.

With further research, we will gain a deeper understanding of the physiological functions and anti-disease mechanisms of Bifidobacteria. In the future, the methods of using _Bifidobacterium_ to alleviate IBD and other diseases will be more scientific and effective.

## 2.1.3 Streptococcus

_Streptococcus_ belongs to the genus of Gram-positive coccus, which can be divided into aerobic, facultatively anaerobic, and microaerophilic types. Typically in chains, they can spread into the environment or colonize the mucous membranes and skin[40]. It is widely distributed in the nasopharynx, gastrointestinal tract, and other parts of nature and the human body. Current research focuses on _Streptococcus thermophilus_, in addition to its good fermentation properties, it also can produce active substances such as extracellular polysaccharides (EPS), bacteriocin, etc.[41]. These metabolites can also inhibit the growth of harmful bacteria, thus alleviating children’s diarrhea, IBD, etc. For example, Chen et al.[42] found that water-soluble exopolysaccharide isolated from _S. hermophilus_ MN-BM-A01 alleviated colitis in mice. Studies have shown that _S_. _thermophilus_ CRL1190 adheres to the gastric mucosa, reduces the adhesive effect of _Helicobacter pylori_, and alleviates the inflammatory response of gastric epithelial cells[43]. In addition, conventional IBD treatments tend to be systemic and the immunosuppressive effects leave the patient more susceptible to infection. Studies have shown that _S_. _thermophilus_ NCIMB 41856 may reduce this immunosuppression[22]. The authors found that _S_. _thermophilus_ NCIMB41856 can reduce bacterial translocation by promoting the maintenance of mucosal barrier function in colitis mice, thereby reducing immune stimulation and associated inflammation.

There are fewer clinical studies of _S. thermophilus_ alleviating IBD, as a potentially beneficial bacterium, its symbiotic mechanism, anti-inflammatory and other properties may be further researched in the future through the latest biotechnology and multidisciplinary intersections.

## 2.1.4 Other bacterial genera

Besides the above probiotics, some strains of the genus _Bacillus_ also belong to a class of probiotics, which have a certain alleviate effect on IBD. _Bacillus_ can be widely found in various natural environments, and most bacteria of the genus _Bacillus_ are harmless. Zhang et al.[44] found that _Bacillus subtilis_ R179 improved DSS-induced malnutrition and intestinal inflammation by balancing gut microbiota and related anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory factors in UC mice, and helped to restore intestinal mucosal damage. Yang et al.[45] found that _B_. _coagulans_ embedded in calcium tungstate microgel (CTM) promoted probiotic colonization, restored intestinal barrier function, and had remarkable anti-inflammatory effects. This research may provide new insights into the colonization of the gut by probiotics for the alleviation of a variety of diseases. Certain commensal microorganisms in the gut have shown anti-inflammatory capacity in different diseases and are considered potential novel probiotics, such as _Akkermansia muciniphila_ (Akk) and _F. prausnitzii_. Sokol et al.[46] conducted _in vivo_ and _in vitro_ experiments and showed that metabolites secreted by _F_. _prausnitzii_ blocked the production of the anti-inflammatory factor IL-8, thereby reducing inflammation, showed that using _F_. _prausnitzi_ as probiotics to balance the ecological imbalance a desirable CD treatment strategy. These studies suggest that gut commensal microorganisms/probiotics are promising therapeutic strategies for IBD, and thus are valuable for the development and utilization of their resources.

As one of the most common bacteria in life, _E_. _coli_ Nissle 1917 (EcN) is often used to do various studies. For example, EcN could promote the recovery of colitis by activating the TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway[47]. Zhang et al.[48] embedded EcN in a colloid consisting of tannic acid (TA) and amino-modified poly-_β_-cyclodextrin. The encapsulated probiotics were highly resistant to the simulated gastrointestinal environment. _In vitro_ and _in vivo_ experiments have confirmed the colloids (NTc) embedding of probiotics in colitis models in mice intestinal adhesion, continuous proliferation activity, and excellent treatment effect. Yang et al.[49] inspired by mucin physiological, with mucin and tannins to the embedding of EcN build the super probiotics strategy (EcN@TA-Ca 2+@Mucin). Mucins can defend against the harsh environment of the gastrointestinal tract and enhance the adhesion of probiotics by interacting with mucus. In addition, the EcN@TA-Ca 2+@Mucin can remove ROS significantly cut inflammation, and improve the abundance and diversity of gut microbiota. Although many studies have demonstrated that EcN is effective in mouse models of colitis induced by DSS or TNBS, it remains to be determined whether this intervention can alleviate pre-existing colitis or be effective in chronic preclinical colitis models.

## 2.2 Mixed probiotics applications

In addition to the application of single probiotics, mixed probiotics have also shown promising results in the alleviation of IBD. For example, Jang et al.[25] found that _L. fermentum_ KBL374 and KBL375 alleviated IBD by affecting immune cytokine expression, microbiome, and metabolic functions, which are desirable novel probiotic candidates for alleviating IBD. VSL#3 is made up of a probiotic mixture of _Bifidobacterium_, _Lactobacillus_, and _S_. _thermophilus_[50]. VSL#3 may be more effective than other single-strain probiotics as which contains a high concentration of 8 different strains of bacteria. Study shows that VSL#3 protects colonic epithelial barrier function in mice with DSS-induced acute colitis[26]. Shi et al.[27] found that mixed _Lactobacillus_ (_L_. _acidophilus_ KLDS 1.0901, _L_. _helveticus_ KLDS 1.8701, and _L_. _plantarum_ KLDS 1.0318) can alleviate DSS-induced colitis by modulating gut microbiota and recovering the intestinal barrier.

Sood et al.[33] used VSL#3 for the treatment of mild-to-moderately active UC and found that VSL#3 alleviated symptoms in clinical patients at week 12 compared to placebo. Bifid Triple Viable Capsule (BTVC) is a mixture of three kinds of probiotics, which are _Bifidobacterium_, _Enterococcus_, and _L. acidophilus_. Wei et al.[34] demonstrated in a clinical study that mesalazine in combination with BTVC can significantly enhance treatment efficacy by mitigating inflammatory injury and oxidative stress reaction in UC patients. In addition, Li et al.[51] demonstrated that mesalazine plus somatostatin and BTVC were effective in improving clinical symptoms in patients with UC.

In conclusion, mixed probiotics have some efficacy in relieving IBD and have better efficacy in relieving UC, but the efficacy of probiotics in IBD varies depending on the type of probiotics, dosage, usage, and duration of treatment, so further experiments are needed to verify the efficacy of probiotics in future.

## 3 Probiotic delivery systems

Probiotics, as a class of microorganisms beneficial to humans, are often used in alleviating IBD. However, the harsh environment of the gastrointestinal tract results in a low survival rate of probiotics, limited retention in the intestinal tract, and inability to achieve precise delivery, all of which greatly restrict probiotics from exerting their biological activities. Probiotics must travel through the mouth (pH 5−7), stomach (pH 1−3), small intestine (pH 6−7.4), and large intestine (pH 6−8) before reaching the colon. All of these areas include threatening factors to the survival of probiotics, decreasing the amount of probiotics that reach the colon, as a result, the survival rate of probiotics is greatly reduced. The tolerance of probiotics to the gastrointestinal environment can be improved by embedding probiotics (Fig. 3), and the efficacy and targeting of the delivery system can also be improved by changing the encapsulation material.

## 3.1 Microencapsulated delivery systems

Microencapsulation technology uses certain techniques to encapsulate probiotics in natural or synthetic polymers to form tiny particles. Many studies have shown that encapsulating probiotics in microgels or other types of microcapsules improves the survival of probiotics[61-63]. An effective microencapsulation system should stabilize the probiotics in storage, protect them from the gastrointestinal tract, and allow for efficient release into the colon and eventual colonization of the mucosal surface. In the embedding technology of microcapsules, the commonly used embedding materials are polysaccharides (chitosan, pectin, alginate), proteins (gelatin, whey proteins), etc., which have high biocompatibility and good thermal stability and are usually used in the embedding of probiotics by extrusion, emulsification, coagulation, and other techniques[64].

## 3.1.1 Biopolymers-embedding probiotic delivery system

The materials used to fabricate microgels are typically biopolymers, the main biopolymers commonly used for embedding are alginate, chitosan, pectin, starch, and proteins, which usually have high biocompatibility, low cost, and low toxicity. Alginate has the advantages of strong encapsulation ability, good biocompatibility, and non-toxicity, and is widely used as a wall material for the production of microcapsules. A recent study has shown that encapsulating _L_. _lactis_ in alginate microcapsules not only resists environmental stresses but also enhances probiotic viability compared to free probiotics[65]. Huq et al.[66] enhanced the survivability of _L_. _rhamnosus_ by encapsulating it within alginate microspheres containing lecithin and cellulose nanoparticles. In addition to alginate, other biopolymers (such as pectin) can also be used as encapsulation materials. Although they are not as widely used as alginate in encapsulating probiotics, they have the potential to serve as a good wall material that protects probiotics from the low pH and bile in the stomach. For example, Li et al.[54] experimentally demonstrated that encapsulation of _L_. _rhamnosus_ in a microgel assembled from pectin could improve its survivability under simulated gastrointestinal tract conditions, exerted higher levels of effects on prevention of DSS-induced colonic injury and colitis and suppression of proinflammatory cytokine production. To enhance probiotic delivery and colonization in the gut, Yang et al.[45] proposed an oral probiotic delivery system based on CTM. CTM promoted probiotic colonization and showed resistance to the harsh environment of the gastrointestinal tract and intestinal adhesions. It was demonstrated that the system was able to significantly alleviate IBD by restoring colonic length, mucosal barrier, and gut microbiota balance.

Compounding multiple biopolymers has been reported to improve encapsulation efficiency, functional properties, and applicability[67]. Thus, in addition to the single embedding materials mentioned above, in some cases, combining two or more biopolymers can enhance their stability or functionality. Pankasemsuk et al.[68] demonstrated that alginate-starch microcapsules increase the survivability of _L_. _casei_ in a simulated gastrointestinal environment. For the past few years, polymers have also been used in the manufacture of microcapsules for the oral administration of probiotics[69]. For example, _γ_-PGA is a component of fermented food slime and a safe edible polymer. By constructing a _γ_-PGA hydrogel microcapsule-embedded probiotic delivery system, Wang et al.[56] demonstrated that the hydrogel microcapsule strategy not only releases probiotics quickly and regulates the balance of gut microbiota, but also significantly improves the therapeutic efficacy of IBD.

## 3.1.2 Biopolymers-coating probiotic delivery system

Coating technology means that individual probiotic cells are encapsulated in a layer of material, rather than multiple probiotic cells embedded in some kind of matrix (e.g. microgel). Coating or incorporating additional materials into alginate microcapsules is a popular direction in the research of probiotic microcapsules, and such coatings can confer other beneficial properties in addition to protecting microorganisms, such as better control of bacterial release[70]. Chavarri et al.[71] microencapsulated _L_. _gardneri_ and _B_. _bifidum_ with alginate and chitosan coatings by simulating gastrointestinal tract, conditions, and showed that coated probiotics had significantly greater survival than uncoated probiotic under simulated gastrointestinal tract conditions. Trabelsi et al.[72] also demonstrated that microcapsules made up of chitosan coatings and CA cores not only increased probiotic survival but also increased the antimicrobial activity of _L_. _plantarum_ TN9 against pathogenic bacteria. The maltodextrin-starch delivery system has also been shown to enhance probiotic viability in a simulated gastrointestinal tract environment[73]. Li et al.[59] produced EcN@PDNI by constructing polydopamine nanoparticular immunosuppressant (PDNI) and embedding EcN with PDNI coating, which showed that PDNI not only protects EcN from the gastrointestinal tract and improves the survival rate, but also achieves alleviation of IBD by modulating the immune response _in vivo_. Sequential deposition of oppositely charged biopolymers onto probiotic surfaces using LbL electrostatic deposition is also a desirable approach. Thomas et al.[74] used oppositely charged polyelectrolyte complexes (chitosan and dextran sulfate) to encapsulate _Saccharomyces boulardii_ by LbL technology to prevent its degradation during gastrointestinal transport and to pH-sensitive delivery systems to controlled release of probiotics to enhance the viability of _S. boulardii._ Cheng et al.[75] constructed an enzyme-triggered fused filament-like microcapsule by combining electrostatic droplets with LbL self-assembly using alginate and fish protein as embedding materials. This microcapsule protects probiotics from acid and bile salts, controls cellular release, aids bacterial adhesion, and ultimately colonizes the proximal colon and distal ileum.

## 3.2 Hydrogel delivery system

Hydrogel is a three-dimensional porous material consisting of physically or chemically cross-linked polymer chains. With ideal hydrophilicity and high permeability to nutrients or oxygen, hydrogels are widely used in delivery systems[76]. The hydrogels used to relieve IBD consist of natural polymers such as HA[77], alginate[78], and chitosan[79], as well as proteins.

## 3.2.1 Alginate-embedding probiotic delivery system

Alginate is a biocompatible and non-toxic polymer that is popularly used as a wall material in delivery systems[80]. Alginate was used to prepare multilayered hydrogel beads to protect the probiotic _B. breve_ from simulated low pH conditions of gastric juice. Li et al.[38] used an emulsion method to encapsulate _B_. _breve_ in spherical CA beads with smooth surfaces, subsequently exposing them and other free cells to simulated gastric fluid conditions. The survival rate of the embedded probiotics was significantly higher than that of the free cells. Alginate-based hydrogels are pH-sensitive. Based on this characterization, a series of pH-sensitive alginate materials were prepared for targeting colonic delivery systems. For example, Mei et al.[81] successfully developed a novel intestinal-targeted carrier consisting of a Ca-alginate/protamine composite shell and a CA-embedded core of _L_. _casei_, which exhibited significant pH-responsive protection and intestinal-targeting characteristics, providing a potential new intestinal-targeted drug delivery system model. Zhou et al.[82] used sodium alginate and chitosan as an effective biofilm to encapsulate the genetically modified EcN, which not only improved the survival rate of the strain in delivery but also ensured its normal expression of superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase (CAT). Oral administration of this engineered probiotic effectively modulates the gut microbiota and reduces inflammation, thereby alleviating IBD in mice.

## 3.2.2 HA-embedding probiotic delivery system

HA is a naturally occurring non-sulfated glycosaminoglycan that has excellent biocompatibility and biodegradability. It is widely used as a wall material for delivery systems[83]. ROS levels are increased in IBD patients, inducing oxidative damage to epithelial tissues, ultimately leading to mucosal damage[84]. Huang et al.[55] developed a HA-based ROS-responsive hydrogel for encapsulation and targeted delivery of probiotics to alleviate IBD. They used methacrylated HA to encapsulate _L_. _reuteri_, and the negatively charged HA-_L_. _reuteri_ hydrogel preferentially adhered to the positively charged inflamed epithelium. At the same time, the inflamed colonic tissue selectively cleaves thioketal linkages, and the excess ROS generated leads to hydrogel degradation and localized probiotic release. Thus, it was demonstrated that the orally administered HA-_L_. _reuteri_ not only effectively alleviated inflammation in DSS colitis mice, but also exerted an appropriate ROS scavenging ability compared with the free strain. Hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) is a toxic gas, and _Salmonella typhimurium_ (ST) is a typical H 2 S-producing enteric pathogen, which was selected by Xiao et al.[53] to study the antimicrobial activity of HA-embedded _L. rhamnosus_ for its antimicrobial activity. It was found that HA can react with H 2 S to inhibit the negative effects caused by H 2 S while releasing intestinal probiotics. The released ST can compete for binding sites with the source pathogens, thus preventing them from binding to the host rather than destroying the bacteria directly. This offers a new and desirable modality for the alleviation of ST-associated colitis with favorable biocompatibility and safety.

## 3.3 Engineered probiotics for the delivery system

How effective a probiotic is usually depends on the strain and the type of disease, but the mechanism of action is often unknown, affecting the development of therapeutic products, engineered probiotics may be a new approach to treating diseases for which there are no existing treatment options. As technology evolves, tools for modifying and editing microorganisms become more advanced and feasible, allowing us to design probiotics as we see fit and thus make them more functional. Engineered probiotics have been targeted for the treatment of several diseases, including diabetes, IBD, and cancer[85]. Human commensal bacteria, especially _Lactococcus, Lactobacillus_, and _E_. _coli_, are a suitable basis for medical engineering[86]. For example, _L_. _lactis_ strains have been modified to express IL-23 receptor blockers on their surface to inhibit pro-inflammatory responses[87]. In addition, _L. lactis_ was modified to secrete the anti-inflammatory factor IL-10 locally in the intestinal tract for its anti-inflammatory effects[88]. In addition to the above-engineered bacteria, EcN is favored for its ease of genetic manipulation and probiotic properties[89]. It is a non-pathogenic strain with no known harmful effects on the host[90].

Some substances, such as anti-tumor necrosis factor and interleukins, were widely used in therapy because of their significant therapeutic effects and ease of synthesis, etc.[88,91]. Therefore, it is possible to engineer EcN to express therapeutic substances to alleviate IBD. For example, patients with IBD lack the antimicrobial peptides _α_-defensin 5 (HD5) and _β_-defensin 2 (HBD2) in the gut, therefore, Seo et al.[92] constructed a plasmid containing HBD2 and converted it into the EcN strain. Besides the effective production of HD5 and HBD2 defensins, the fusion protein secreted by this strain inhibited the growth of _E. coli_ and _Salmonella_, which is a feasible method to alleviate IBD. Praveschotinunt et al.[7] modified EcN so that it could produce a matrix of coiled fibers that had a trichostatin factor (TFF) component that promoted epithelial repair and intestinal barrier function. Modified EcN secretes non-toxic TFF _in vitro_ and _in vivo_. The results showed that engineered EcN had a stronger protective effect on the DSS-induced murine colitis model, suggesting that engineered EcN can produce proteins with protective effects _in situ_. (_R_)-_β_-Hydroxybutyric acid (3HB) is mainly derived from ketone bodies in animals and is a source of energy during starvation or exercise[93]. In addition to its energy supply function, 3HB was also considered a therapeutic drug. Yan et al.[94] inserted the exogenous 3HB synthesis pathway into the EcN genome and utilized EcN for sustained production of 3HB in the intestines of colitis mice. The results showed that the persistent presence of 3HB in the mouse intestine increased the abundance of Akk and produced large amounts of SCFAs, which resulted in the alleviation of inflammation.

## 4 The mechanism of probiotics to alleviate IBD

## 4.1 Maintaining gut microbiota barrier balance

Humans receive their initial gut microbiota from their mothers at birth, and the gut microbiota in infancy is mainly dominated by _Bifidobacterium_. The human body forms a symbiotic relationship with gut microbiota as it grows, which changes based on factors such as environment, diet, and age. Many gastrointestinal diseases are caused by the imbalance of gut microbiota, so the establishment of a relatively balanced microbiota-host interaction is crucial for host health. In the intestines of IBD patients, harmful bacteria such as _Clostridium_ are increased and mucosa-associated beneficial bacteria _Bifidobacterium_ are decreased[95-96]. This suggests that a reasonable control of intestinal bacteria may provide a way of thinking about the alleviation of IBD.

## 4.1.1 Producing antibacterial substances

Probiotics can not only directly affect gut microbiota, but also indirectly regulate metabolites of gut microbiota, such as hydrogen peroxide, bacteriocins, antimicrobial active peptides, and neurotransmitters. For example, lactic acid bacteria and Bifidobacteria may act antimicrobial against pathogens by producing antimicrobial substances (bacteriocins and acids) and by stimulating mucosal immunity[97]. Bacteriocins are bacteria-killing protein molecules synthesized by the ribosome produced by a bacterium and have certain activity[98]. Fukuda et al.[99] showed that protective Bifidobacteria produce acetate, which improves the gut defense and maintains the normal balance of the gut microbiota. Yan et al.[100] targeted delivery of the soluble protein p40 extracted from _L_. _rhamnosus_ to the mice colon. Improved intestinal epithelial cell apoptosis and disruption of barrier function resulted in the alleviation of acute colitis.

## 4.1.2 Strengthening the intestinal mucosal barrier function

The intestinal mucosal barrier is composed primarily of an epithelial cell layer, a mucus layer, and antimicrobial substances produced by the intestinal epithelial cells, which prevents the invasion of pathogenic bacteria. The gastrointestinal epithelium is a major interface to the outside environment. A large number of microorganisms and metabolites adhere to the mucosal surface of the intestinal epithelium[101]. The gastrointestinal epithelium can defend against the invasion of intestinal toxins and bacteria, but due to inflammation, the barrier function of the epithelium is impaired. Epithelial barrier disruption and altered intestinal permeability can be found in patients with IBD, suggesting that the epithelial barrier has an important role in alleviating IBD. The goblet cells in the intestines of UC patients function abnormally and mucus secretion decreases, leading to loss or thinning of the mucus layer, which makes bacteria invade epithelial cells and aggravate the inflammation of the body[102]. This suggests that disruption of mucus and its barrier function _in vivo_ leads to inflammation, and thus restoration and reconstruction of the intestinal barrier may serve as a new strategic pathway to alleviate IBD.

The intestinal mucosal barrier function of mice with colitis is seriously affected, after oral administration of EcN, it can mediate the up-regulation of ZO-1 expression in mouse intestinal epithelial cells and provide protection against the increase of material permeability in the lumen[101]. _L_. _rhamnosus_ CNCMI-3690 can protect the intestinal barrier function in a mouse inflammatory model. By studying its mechanism of action, Martin et al.[103] found that _L_. _rhamnosus_ CNCMI-3690 not only stimulated goblet cells to secrete mucin by inhibiting the increase of intestinal permeability but also maintained the mucus barrier function by regulating the expression of MUC2. An animal study found that _L_. _reuteri_ ATCC PTA 4659 increased the interaction of epithelial structural proteins by increasing the production of epithelial heat shock proteins 25 and 70, which in turn maintained the integrity of the intestinal barrier[104].

It has been demonstrated that a combination of probiotics provides better benefits and better efficacy in alleviating IBD. For example, the probiotic mixture VSL#3 can protect the epithelial barrier by maintaining the expression of tight junction proteins Occludin, ZO-1, etc., and inhibiting apoptosis[26]. Studies have shown that VSL#3 can increase IL-10 and reduce the expression of IL-12p40 and Toll-like receptor-2 in intestinal DC of UC patients[105]. Probiotics also have been known to suppress pro-inflammatory factors, such as _L_. _rhamnosus_, which decreased TNF-α production by lipopolysaccharide-activated mouse macrophages[106]. Besides the direct interaction between immune cells and probiotics, the DNA in probiotics also modulates immune function in humans and mice. For example, Jijon et al.[107] found that DNA isolated from VSL#3 reduced the release of TNF, IL-8, and IFN-γ both _in vitro_ and _in vivo_. This suggests that probiotic DNA inhibits pro-inflammatory responses and that oral administration of this VSL#3 DNA can improve inflammatory responses.

## 4.2 Modulating the immune response

Dysregulated immune responses, consisting of adaptive and innate immunity, play a critical role in IBD. Some probiotics promote T cell differentiation, regulating cell factors and intestinal IgA+ cell level to promote the host’s innate immunity and adaptive immunity[108], therefore, keeping a balance between essential and excessive defense mechanisms is a key to IBD alleviation. Human gastrointestinal mucosal immune control causes IBD, and the intestinal immune cytokines and signaling pathways have a significant role in the pathogenesis of IBD[109]. IL-10 is an interleukin produced by many types of immune cells, such as T cells (CD4+ T cells and CD8+ T cells), B cells, phagocytes (macrophages and neutrophils), DC, natural killer cells, etc.[110], it can inhibit proinflammatory and adaptive immune cells and helps maintain mucosal homeostasis. In an animal model, _B. infantis_ increased the production of the anti-inflammatory factors transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) and IL-10 and decreased several pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-23, IL-17, and IL-12)[111]. Probiotics can induce adaptive immunity by activating innate immunity and further modulate immune cells and signaling pathways to regulate the immune response, reduce pro-inflammatory factors, and increase anti-inflammatory factors to achieve the purpose of reducing inflammation[112-113] (Fig. 4). For example, Furusawa et al.[114] found that _Clostridium leptum_, a dominant class of commensal microbes, can promote Foxp3 expression by producing butyrate, leading to the differentiation of initial CD4+ T cells into Treg cells, thereby reducing the occurrence of inflammation.

## 4.3 Alleviating oxidative stress

ROS is a collective term used to describe the chemicals formed when oxygen is incompletely reduced, consisting primarily of hydroxyl radical (HO·), superoxide anion (O 2-·), and hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2)[115]. Oxidative stress has a significant effect on IBD pathogenesis, in which ROS is not only a by-product of aerobic metabolism but also a key molecule in physiological processes[116-117]. Endogenous ROS at low levels in the human body may contribute to the maintenance of normal physiological functions[118], however, excessive ROS can lead to oxidative stress, which can exacerbate the inflammatory response. Particularly in the gastrointestinal tract, this can lead to damage to the intestinal mucosal layer and invasion of pathogens, which can stimulate an immune response and ultimately lead to IBD[119]. Probiotics can be used as potential natural antioxidants that have a significant effect in decreasing oxidative stress and exhibit strong antioxidant activity in the host gut[120].

Nowak et al.[121] found that _Lactobacillus_ and _Bifidobacterium_ enhanced antioxidant enzyme activity promoted the production of substances with antioxidant activity (extracellular polysaccharide, glutathione, etc.), and prevented the formation of toxic superoxide anions. In addition, they have ROS-binding systems and metal-chelating activities that decrease oxidative stress, subsequently reducing membrane lipid peroxidation, protein damage, and repairing DNA. ROS plays a crucial role in gut inflammation; therefore, scavenging of ROS at the site of inflammation by antioxidant enzymes such as SOD and CAT is effective in inhibiting IBD. _L_. _casei_ BL23 was shown to significantly increase intestinal enzyme activities and decrease inflammatory responses in TNBS-induced CD model mice by producing SOD and CAT[122]. In addition, Bifidobacteria increases the expression of antioxidant enzymes such as glutathione peroxidase, CAT, and SOD, which help to scavenge ROS from the host’s intestinal tract, thereby mitigating oxidative damage. For example, _B_. _longum_ was used as a carrier of superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) to decrease ROS associated with UC. The penetrating protein PEP-1 was fused to the potent anti-inflammatory but poorly permeable and stable antioxidant enzyme MnSOD for transport into host cells. The study suggests probiotics successfully express therapeutic proteins to alleviate symptoms in UC mice[123].

In summary, IBD is a very complex disease whose direct etiology and pathomechanisms are not fully understood. A large number of studies have shown that probiotics can regulate or alleviate IBD, but there are few rigorous clinical studies on probiotics and the results are unsatisfactory, so probiotics have not been used on a wide scale.

## 5 Conclusion & future perspectives

With the incidence of IBD gradually increasing in recent years and the side effects of conventional drug therapy, the use of probiotics to alleviate IBD has received increasing attention. Genetic susceptibility factors, environmental factors, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and immune disorders are the pathogenesis of IBD. Probiotic drug delivery systems are frequently used to alleviate IBD because of their anti-inflammatory and gut microbiota regulation effects. However, either system will have certain drawbacks, so there are still some challenges and opportunities on the way to building a probiotic delivery system.

(1) The development of microencapsulation materials is becoming more and more diversified, and microencapsulation not only effectively improves the activity of probiotics and stability during storage, but also protects its arrival in the colon through the digestive tract and improves the ability of live bacteria to colonize the mucous membranes on the intestinal surface. However, microencapsulation technology also faces many challenges. For example, the preparation of embedded wall materials needs to avoid ingredients or processes that adversely affect probiotic viability, such as excessive heating, strong acids or bases, and surfactants. Therefore, besides needing to create probiotic strains that are thermally stable and strong, new encapsulation techniques need to be developed to improve their heat resistance. Additionally, some probiotic delivery systems do not give adequate protection during storage and transportation, which can lead to probiotic degradation. These are issues that remain to be addressed.

(2) As a good wall material, hydrogel has the advantages of controlled and prolonged release time and localized drug delivery. Therefore, hydrogels used for therapeutic purposes should have good biocompatibility as well as non-toxicity. Furthermore, how to minimize or eliminate the side effects resulting from the biodegradation of hydrogels is also a problem that needs to be overcome.

(3) Engineered strains have great potential to diagnose and alleviate different diseases, with the advantages of site-specific drug delivery, sustainable release, and mechanism-controlled therapy. In the future, it may become a new way to alleviate diseases such as cancer. Even so, it still has some challenges. For example, while humans have studied and engineered quite a few microorganisms, this is still only a small fraction of a large family of microorganisms, and many microorganisms have virtually no manipulable genetic tools, which has resulted in probiotic modifications being limited to a small number of strains. In addition, in today’s society, there are still some people who believe that genetically modified organisms are harmful, which hinders the development of engineered strains.

In conclusion, this paper describes the different types of probiotics, delivery systems, and anti-inflammatory therapeutic effects, which need to be followed up with further exploration of the potential mechanisms by which probiotic delivery systems work. For the components of different wall materials and the molecular mechanisms and signaling pathways that produce their effects, their application safety also requires more systematic and comprehensive evaluation. With the rapid development of society, the pathogenesis of IBD will be studied more thoroughly, and there is an urgent need to investigate delivery systems constructed through new strategies. On the one hand, we need to establish more rigorous randomized, double-blind, and placebo trials to verify the clinical value of probiotics; on the other hand, we need to further study the mechanism of probiotics to alleviate IBD, so that we can use appropriate probiotic preparations for the treatment of patients with IBD at different stages and with different symptoms. In addition to alleviating IBD, probiotics should be used further for broader aspects such as alleviating colon cancer and tumors. Going forward, probiotics are expected to be designed as more convenient, safer, and more effective treatments for a wider range of diseases.

## Highlights

• Probiotics alleviate IBD through different mechanisms of action.

• Free probiotics are easily degraded during processing and digestion.

• The delivery system enhances the biological activity of probiotics.

• Probiotics for alleviating IBD were introduced to the intestine attributed to the different probiotic delivery systems.

• Engineered probiotic delivery is a novel approach to alleviating IBD.

## Abstract

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) influences several million people around the globe, with a high prevalence in North America and Europe. Results from the studies about host-gut microbial interactions demonstrated that gut microbiota plays a critical role in the progression of IBD, and probiotics can significantly improve microflora dysbiosis and inflammatory response caused by intestinal pathogens. However, several limitations existed for the probiotics delivered to the intestine in the free form (non-encapsulated), such as low pH and diverse digestive enzymes in the gastrointestinal tract, etc. To overcome the problems, several probiotic delivery systems were established and verified with effects. Here, the types and applications of probiotics in animal models and clinical studies are first reviewed in this paper. Subsequently, various types of probiotic delivery systems are elaborated, containing the well-known microcapsules and hydrogel delivery systems, and the engineered probiotic delivery systems are also introduced. Furthermore, mechanisms of action associated with probiotics are illustrated, including maintaining gut microbiota barrier balance, modulating the immune response, and alleviating oxidative stress, etc. Finally, we discussed the relative advantages and disadvantages of different encapsulation methods, as well as future trends for further development of probiotic delivery systems with health benefits.

## 1 Introduction

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic intestinal disease known as progressive, nonspecific, and recurrent, which induces long-term inflammation of the colon and can lead to the symptoms of fever vomiting, persistent diarrhea, as well as abdominal pain. In addition, another feature of IBD is abnormal feces, which may contain blood and mucus. The IBD can be divided into two types, including Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC)[1], according to the lesion locations. The lesions of UC are mainly confined to the inflammation of rectal and colon mucosa and submucosa, showing continuous and diffuse distribution[2]; CD lesions are marked by segmental in flammation which can involve anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract, but most often involve the distal ileum[3]. Most IBD patients are between 33 and 39 years old[4], and this seriously affects their quality of life and daily life, resulting in increased medical costs. Since the 21 st century, with the rapid development of urbanization and social economy, there has been a dramatic rise in the prevalence of IBD around the world[5]. The causes of IBD are still unclear, but is widely recognized to be related to several factors, such as genetics, immune imbalance, intestinal microecological imbalance, diet, environment, and other factors[6].

Traditional drug therapies for IBD are non-targeted, and commonly used medications include aminosalicylic acid, glucocorticoids, antibiotics, corticosteroids, and immunosuppressants. These drugs inhibit inflammation by reducing the opportunities for bacterial infection of mucosal wounds[7].

It has been demonstrated that patients with IBD have changes in the intestinal microenvironment, including imbalances in the gut microbiota and increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which ultimately lead to intestinal mucosal damage[8]. A genetic catalog of the microbial species that inhabit a defined environment such as the human body is called the microbiome[9], and unlike the human genome, which is rarely altered by external intervention, intestinal microbiota compositions are readily altered through diet, pathogen infections, antibiotic intake, as well as other life events. When the balance of the human gut is out of whack, it can lead to intestinal diseases and complications. There are a variety of probiotics in the human gut microbiota, including _Lactobacillus_, _Bifidobacterium_, _Streptococcus_, etc. These probiotics can alleviate IBD and promote human health through mechanisms such as maintaining the balance of gut microbiota and regulating cytokine secretion[10]. Therefore, delivering probiotics is an effective way to alleviate IBD. However, oral (non-embedded) probiotics are easily degraded by the harsh conditions within the human gastrointestinal tract, including the low pH in the stomach, as well as the bile salts and digestive enzymes in the small intestine[11]. It is necessary to establish a targeted delivery system that protects probiotics from degradation. Here, we collected 1179 research articles focusing on probiotics and IBD from 2019 to 2023 by searching the Web of Science database, and the keyword co-occurrence network diagram shows that the probiotic delivery system for the alleviation of IBD has been widely used in mouse models, clinical double-blind trials, and other fields (Fig. 1). In addition, the research mainly focuses on probiotic species, mechanisms, and applications. Here, we focus on three probiotics (_Lactobacillus_, _Bifidobacterium_, and _Streptococcus_) that can alleviate IBD.

Based on the recent research progress of probiotic delivery systems in the alleviation of IBD, this paper firstly introduced the types and applications of probiotics in animal models and clinical studies. ## 2 Therapeutic applications of probiotics in IBD

Appropriate probiotic dose administration has positive effects on host organisms. Studies showed that the probiotic species that can alleviate IBD mainly contain _Lactobacillus_, _Bifidobacterium_, _Streptococcus_, etc. (Table 1), and also include mixed probiotics. Some of these are mainly derived from yogurt, cheese, pickles, kefir, sourdough bread, fermented bean curd, tempeh, etc. These probiotics have many benefits for the body (Fig. 2). These probiotic strains are effective in alleviating IBD, either in mouse or rat disease models or in clinical studies (Tables 1 and 2). Dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) and 2,4,6-trinitrobenzene sulfonic acid (TNBS) are often used to induce colitis in animal models. DSS is mainly used to induce UC, and TNBS is widely used to induce CD[12].

## 2.1 Single probiotics applications

## 2.1.1 Lactobacillus

_Lactobacillus_ belongs to Gram-positive bacteria, which can be divided into obligate anaerobic, facultative anaerobic, or microaerophilic types[35]. At present, the common _Lactobacillus_ species include _L_. _plantarum_, _L_. _rhamnosus_, _L_. _acidophilus_, and others. Plenty of animal studies have demonstrated that these _Lactobacillus_ have effects on alleviating colitis in mice. For example, Zan et al.[16] found that _L_. _plantarum_ 6076 had a significant alleviating effect on DSS-induced colitis. It not only alters the composition of the gut microbiota but also reduces inflammation by reducing oxidative stress. This study provides novel insights into the alleviation of IBD and holds potential clinical applications. Liu et al.[17] experimentally demonstrated that _L_. _valerate_ YQ001 and _L_. _advancedus_ YQ005 were able to reduce the expression levels of pro-inflammatory factors IL-1β and IL-6 and improve the gut microbiota. This suggests that these two strains have anti-inflammatory effects, and also provide new insights and new resources for the development of food-based therapies for chronic diseases.

In children with UC, mucosal inflammation can be effectively alleviated by the administration of _L_. _reuteri_ ATCC 55730, which alters the expression levels of cytokines affecting IBD[28]. In colonic mucosa of patients with mild UC, D’Incà et al.[29] found that rectal administration of _L_. _casei_ DG modifies not only pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β and TNF-α levels decreased and anti-inflammatory factor IL-10 increased, but also improves the colonic microbiota (_Lactobacillus_ increased, Enterobacteriaceae decreased). Within the patient-based studies, Hegazy et al.[30] found that _L._ _fermentum_ not only reduced NF-κB DNA binding activity, but also reduced leukocyte accumulation and down-regulated IL-6 and TNF-α production, thereby alleviating the severity of colitis.

In general, _Lactobacillus_ shows potential as an intervention for IBD. It can modulate the immune response, reduce inflammation, etc., but further research is needed to better understand the mechanisms of beneficial effects of _Lactobacillus_ and to determine the optimal strains and dosages for use in patients with IBD clinical treatment.

## 2.1.2 Bifidobacterium

_Bifidobacterium_ belongs to Gram-positive bacteria and anaerobic type. Among them, _Bifidobacterium_ is a V-shaped or Y-shaped branch of Bifidobacteriaceae and Actinobacteria, which is distributed throughout the intestinal tract of animals and humans. It maintains intestinal microecological balance, immunomodulation, and antimicrobial activity[36]. _Bifidobacterium_, as a representative class of probiotics in the human gastrointestinal tract, not only has obvious therapeutic effects but also has the advantage of having fewer side effects, etc. _B_. _infantis_ is a type of probiotic normally found in the human gut. It can alter the balance of gut microbiota in the gastrointestinal tract, thus helping to reduce inflammation. Such as, it has been demonstrated that _B_. _infantis_ not only promotes the recovery of inflammatory tissues in the TNBS model of rat colitis but also supports the maintenance of colonic integrity against chronic inflammatory processes[18]. This shows that _B_. _infantis_ has an important role in maintaining colon morphology. Modulation of gut microbiota also gives us inspiration for preventing and alleviating IBD through dietary modifications.

_B_. _breve_ M-16V is a probiotic with a long tradition of use in neonatal intensive care units in some countries. Izumi et al.[37] induced colitis in rats with DSS and then found that _B. breve_ M-16V had a certain alleviating effect on colitis in weaned rats. Thus, this strain is considered a safe strain to use not only in neonatal infants but also in weaning children. _Bifidobacterium_ has better intestinal tolerance than other species such as _Lactobacillus_, but in some cases, embedding it can also enhance its vitality and play a better role. For example, Li et al.[38] encapsulated _B. breve_ in spherical calcium alginate (CA) beads with a smooth surface by the emulsion method and then simulated various pH environments in the gastrointestinal tract. It demonstrated a remarkable increase in the viability of the encapsulated _B. breve_. Wang et al.[39] embedded probiotics with hyaluronic acid-bilirubin nanomedicine (HABN). The synthesized BL@HABN not only reduced pro-inflammatory factors and repaired the epithelial barrier, but also restored the abundance and diversity of the intestinal microbiota.

Within the patient-based studies, Tamaki et al.[31] demonstrated in a clinical study that _B_. _longum_ 536 improved the clinical symptoms of UC patients. In addition, Groeger et al.[32] demonstrated that _B. infantis_ 35624 can reduce the levels of C-reactive protein and the pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-6 in UC patients. Although the efficacy of _Bifidobacterium_ in the alleviation of IBD is well established, further research is needed to confirm the efficacy and safety of probiotic therapy in clinical studies.

With further research, we will gain a deeper understanding of the physiological functions and anti-disease mechanisms of Bifidobacteria. In the future, the methods of using _Bifidobacterium_ to alleviate IBD and other diseases will be more scientific and effective.

## 2.1.3 Streptococcus

_Streptococcus_ belongs to the genus of Gram-positive coccus, which can be divided into aerobic, facultatively anaerobic, and microaerophilic types. Typically in chains, they can spread into the environment or colonize the mucous membranes and skin[40]. It is widely distributed in the nasopharynx, gastrointestinal tract, and other parts of nature and the human body. Current research focuses on _Streptococcus thermophilus_, in addition to its good fermentation properties, it also can produce active substances such as extracellular polysaccharides (EPS), bacteriocin, etc.[41]. These metabolites can also inhibit the growth of harmful bacteria, thus alleviating children’s diarrhea, IBD, etc. For example, Chen et al.[42] found that water-soluble exopolysaccharide isolated from _S. hermophilus_ MN-BM-A01 alleviated colitis in mice. Studies have shown that _S_. _thermophilus_ CRL1190 adheres to the gastric mucosa, reduces the adhesive effect of _Helicobacter pylori_, and alleviates the inflammatory response of gastric epithelial cells[43]. In addition, conventional IBD treatments tend to be systemic and the immunosuppressive effects leave the patient more susceptible to infection. Studies have shown that _S_. _thermophilus_ NCIMB 41856 may reduce this immunosuppression[22]. The authors found that _S_. _thermophilus_ NCIMB41856 can reduce bacterial translocation by promoting the maintenance of mucosal barrier function in colitis mice, thereby reducing immune stimulation and associated inflammation.

There are fewer clinical studies of _S. thermophilus_ alleviating IBD, as a potentially beneficial bacterium, its symbiotic mechanism, anti-inflammatory and other properties may be further researched in the future through the latest biotechnology and multidisciplinary intersections.

## 2.1.4 Other bacterial genera

Besides the above probiotics, some strains of the genus _Bacillus_ also belong to a class of probiotics, which have a certain alleviate effect on IBD. _Bacillus_ can be widely found in various natural environments, and most bacteria of the genus _Bacillus_ are harmless. Zhang et al.[44] found that _Bacillus subtilis_ R179 improved DSS-induced malnutrition and intestinal inflammation by balancing gut microbiota and related anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory factors in UC mice, and helped to restore intestinal mucosal damage. Yang et al.[45] found that _B_. _coagulans_ embedded in calcium tungstate microgel (CTM) promoted probiotic colonization, restored intestinal barrier function, and had remarkable anti-inflammatory effects. This research may provide new insights into the colonization of the gut by probiotics for the alleviation of a variety of diseases. Certain commensal microorganisms in the gut have shown anti-inflammatory capacity in different diseases and are considered potential novel probiotics, such as _Akkermansia muciniphila_ (Akk) and _F. prausnitzii_. Sokol et al.[46] conducted _in vivo_ and _in vitro_ experiments and showed that metabolites secreted by _F_. _prausnitzii_ blocked the production of the anti-inflammatory factor IL-8, thereby reducing inflammation, showed that using _F_. _prausnitzi_ as probiotics to balance the ecological imbalance a desirable CD treatment strategy. These studies suggest that gut commensal microorganisms/probiotics are promising therapeutic strategies for IBD, and thus are valuable for the development and utilization of their resources.

As one of the most common bacteria in life, _E_. _coli_ Nissle 1917 (EcN) is often used to do various studies. For example, EcN could promote the recovery of colitis by activating the TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway[47]. Zhang et al.[48] embedded EcN in a colloid consisting of tannic acid (TA) and amino-modified poly-_β_-cyclodextrin. The encapsulated probiotics were highly resistant to the simulated gastrointestinal environment. _In vitro_ and _in vivo_ experiments have confirmed the colloids (NTc) embedding of probiotics in colitis models in mice intestinal adhesion, continuous proliferation activity, and excellent treatment effect. Yang et al.[49] inspired by mucin physiological, with mucin and tannins to the embedding of EcN build the super probiotics strategy (EcN@TA-Ca 2+@Mucin). Mucins can defend against the harsh environment of the gastrointestinal tract and enhance the adhesion of probiotics by interacting with mucus. In addition, the EcN@TA-Ca 2+@Mucin can remove ROS significantly cut inflammation, and improve the abundance and diversity of gut microbiota. Although many studies have demonstrated that EcN is effective in mouse models of colitis induced by DSS or TNBS, it remains to be determined whether this intervention can alleviate pre-existing colitis or be effective in chronic preclinical colitis models.

## 2.2 Mixed probiotics applications

In addition to the application of single probiotics, mixed probiotics have also shown promising results in the alleviation of IBD. For example, Jang et al.[25] found that _L. fermentum_ KBL374 and KBL375 alleviated IBD by affecting immune cytokine expression, microbiome, and metabolic functions, which are desirable novel probiotic candidates for alleviating IBD. VSL#3 is made up of a probiotic mixture of _Bifidobacterium_, _Lactobacillus_, and _S_. _thermophilus_[50]. VSL#3 may be more effective than other single-strain probiotics as which contains a high concentration of 8 different strains of bacteria. Study shows that VSL#3 protects colonic epithelial barrier function in mice with DSS-induced acute colitis[26]. Shi et al.[27] found that mixed _Lactobacillus_ (_L_. _acidophilus_ KLDS 1.0901, _L_. _helveticus_ KLDS 1.8701, and _L_. _plantarum_ KLDS 1.0318) can alleviate DSS-induced colitis by modulating gut microbiota and recovering the intestinal barrier.

Sood et al.[33] used VSL#3 for the treatment of mild-to-moderately active UC and found that VSL#3 alleviated symptoms in clinical patients at week 12 compared to placebo. Bifid Triple Viable Capsule (BTVC) is a mixture of three kinds of probiotics, which are _Bifidobacterium_, _Enterococcus_, and _L. acidophilus_. Wei et al.[34] demonstrated in a clinical study that mesalazine in combination with BTVC can significantly enhance treatment efficacy by mitigating inflammatory injury and oxidative stress reaction in UC patients. In addition, Li et al.[51] demonstrated that mesalazine plus somatostatin and BTVC were effective in improving clinical symptoms in patients with UC.

In conclusion, mixed probiotics have some efficacy in relieving IBD and have better efficacy in relieving UC, but the efficacy of probiotics in IBD varies depending on the type of probiotics, dosage, usage, and duration of treatment, so further experiments are needed to verify the efficacy of probiotics in future.

## 3 Probiotic delivery systems

Probiotics, as a class of microorganisms beneficial to humans, are often used in alleviating IBD. However, the harsh environment of the gastrointestinal tract results in a low survival rate of probiotics, limited retention in the intestinal tract, and inability to achieve precise delivery, all of which greatly restrict probiotics from exerting their biological activities. Probiotics must travel through the mouth (pH 5−7), stomach (pH 1−3), small intestine (pH 6−7.4), and large intestine (pH 6−8) before reaching the colon. All of these areas include threatening factors to the survival of probiotics, decreasing the amount of probiotics that reach the colon, as a result, the survival rate of probiotics is greatly reduced. The tolerance of probiotics to the gastrointestinal environment can be improved by embedding probiotics (Fig. 3), and the efficacy and targeting of the delivery system can also be improved by changing the encapsulation material.
